items.title: Human Situational Awareness and Workload during Heterogeneous Autonomous Vehicle Hazard Monitoring: A Cross-Platform Study
items.abstract: As autonomous ground and aerial vehicles become increasingly capable, human operators are transitioning from direct control to supervisory monitoring roles. Maintaining Situational Awareness (SA) during rare but safety critical hazard events remains a fundamental challenge, particularly when operators must monitor heterogeneous autonomous platforms with different spatial and cognitive demands. This study develops a unified experimental framework for investigating human SA and workload during supervisory monitoring of autonomous ground and aerial vehicles under hazard conditions. Eighteen participants completed six within-subject conditions combining three interface modalities, namely, visual-only, haptic-only, and visual-haptic, with two platform types, ground vehicle and aerial drone. SA was measured using Situation Awareness Rating Technique (SART), while workload was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). The key findings are: 1) Aerial monitoring produced significantly lower overall SA, higher situational demand, and greater workload than ground monitoring, driven by elevated Demand and reduced Understanding rather than diminished Supply. 2) Workload was consistently coupled with situational demand across all conditions, suggesting a stable SA-workload mechanism. 3) Both haptic-only and visual-haptic significantly improved overall SA relative to visual-only without increasing workload, demonstrating that interface design can enhance awareness within the existing workload envelope. These findings establish a cross-platform behavioural baseline for designing multimodal interfaces that enhance operator SA without elevating workload in heterogeneous autonomous vehicle systems.

items.title: Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence in Health Professions Education and Decision-Making
items.abstract: This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI) transforms health professions education and clinical decision-making through human-centered and sociotechnical systems (STSs) principles. It defines four key affordances (informational, inferential, relational, and organizational) that determine how AI affects learning, collaboration, and care. In education, AI can enhance competency-based medical education through adaptive learning, simulation, and automated assessment, expanding educators’ capacity for feedback and curriculum improvement. In clinical practice, AI can support diagnosis, risk prediction, and workflow coordination but requires transparency, validation, and ethical oversight to maintain trust and professional autonomy. Case studies such as Google Flu Trends and IBM Watson for Oncology show that most failures arise from poor implementation rather than technical limitations. Integrating human-centered design and STS frameworks, the chapter emphasizes the need for co-design, cybersecurity awareness, and accountability as central for effective innovation, ensuring AI supports and enhances human judgment and professional practice rather than replacing or undermining them.

items.title: Human–AI Task Redistribution in Higher Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is redistributing academic work among humans, AI, and human–AI collaboration, raising questions about which tasks learners should continue performing independently. This mixed-methods study examined task allocation using survey data from 317 university students representing 974 recurring academic tasks and interviews with 24 faculty members across 24 disciplines. Student data showed substantial movement from human-only performance toward joint human–AI and AI-delegated work. Task redistribution was significantly associated with perceived skill demands and learning opportunities. Faculty strongly supported preserving independent practice for foundational, embodied, and high-stakes activities while permitting AI for appropriate peripheral, advanced, and efficiency-oriented tasks. Integrating both datasets produced a Human–AI Task Allocation Model organized around a Training Zone–Performance Zone principle. The findings suggest that appropriate AI delegation should depend on learners’ developmental stage, task purpose, and retained capacity for verification, judgment, and accountability.

items.title: HYENAISM: An Emergent Concept in the Political, Social, and Cultural Domains
items.abstract: HYENAISM An Emergent Concept in the Political, Social, and Cultural Domains Ali Jabar Rashidi Professor, Visiting Faculty Member, Supreme National Defense University, Iran Email: a.j.rashidi@gmail.com ORCID: 0009-0006-0371-1408 October 12, 2026 Abstract Exclusively self-interested behavior and actions that disregard humanistic and ethical boundaries are increasingly emerging and spreading among certain individuals, organizations, groups, and countries across various social, political, economic, cultural, and even scientific and technological domains, at local, national, and particularly international levels, including relations among states. Such conduct, which has historically been regarded as unacceptable within human societies, appears to be gaining a degree of normalization and legitimacy. Since these forms of convergence often cross humanistic and ethical boundaries and cannot be clearly captured within conventional classifications of human behavior and action, I propose the term “Hyenaism” to describe this phenomenon, based on my examination and study of its characteristics. Hyenaism is a proposed term for describing opportunistic convergence among actors who, under other circumstances, may be rivals, adversaries, or distrustful of one another. These actors align themselves around shared material or non-material interests and objectives, or a combination of both. To advance such convergence, they may collectively mobilize or exploit a range of capabilities and resources, institutions, laws and rules, narratives, and forms of power. The duration and life cycle of such convergence are not fixed; rather, they depend on the continuation of shared interests and on whether the expected benefits remain at an acceptable level for the participating actors. This original conceptual note presents the definition and conceptual dimensions of Hyenaism as proposed by the author, with the aim of making the concept available for use by researchers and other interested parties. Keywords: Hyenaism; Opportunism; Tactical Alliance; Collective Self-Interest; Institutional Power; Coalition Life Cycle. 1. Definition of Hyenaism Hyenaism is a political, economic, social, military, and cultural pattern of brazen opportunism and collective self-interest in which individuals, groups, countries, political parties, formal or informal organizations, and local, national, or international institutions—which may ordinarily be enemies or rivals—temporarily or conditionally converge to achieve a shared goal, pursue common interests, seize an opportunity, or capture common prey. Shared interests and objectives may be material, non-material, or a combination of both. To facilitate this convergence, participants may coordinate, employ, manipulate, or exploit available instruments and capabilities, including military, political, and economic power; consensus-building and influencing public opinion at local, national, and international levels; mass mobilization; various organizations and institutions; laws, rules, and procedures; culture; poverty, vulnerability, and dependency; science and technology; and other available resources and means. The defining characteristic is not the mere presence of any particular instrument, but rather the opportunistic and potentially exploitative coordination of efforts to secure a common benefit—even when the participants have a history of hostility toward one another or lack enduring friendship and shared values. 2. Scope and Types of Actors in Hyenaism The actors involved in Hyenaism are not limited to individuals or informal groups. They may include any of the following, or combinations thereof: · Individuals, networks, factions, and social groups; · Political parties, movements, and coalitions; · Countries, government bodies, and public officials; · Formal and informal organizations and institutions at local, national, and international levels; · Cross-sectoral coalitions comprising governmental, non-governmental, economic, cultural, scientific, or other actors. This term constitutes an analytical framework and should not be applied indiscriminately to every alliance or form of cooperation. Its application to a specific case requires evidence of opportunistic convergence, the role of shared interests, and the coordinated use of leverage and capabilities. One of its distinguishing features is insufficient adherence to humanistic and ethical considerations in the objectives, methods, and actions associated with the convergence. Hyenaism may constitute the hidden face of certain forms of convergence whose publicly visible and declared image presents purportedly humanitarian and ethical objectives, including opposition to oppression, even when such claims are fabricated or contrived. Consequently, identifying Hyenaism is a strategic undertaking that depends on sufficient situational awareness and a comprehensive intelligence picture. 3. The Nature of Shared Interests and Objectives in Hyenaism The interests and objectives that bring actors together may be material—such as wealth, territory, resources (for example, energy resources, oil, water, and the like, in the case of countries), market access, commercial objectives, or institutional superiority—or non-material, such as sovereign domination, colonization, subordination through dependency, status, legitimacy, influence, identity, and cultural or religious interests. They may also involve a combination of both. The expected benefits do not have to be exactly the same for all participants; in some cases, it is sufficient for each participant to perceive some benefit for themselves arising from the convergence and its temporary arrangements. In certain Hyenaism scenarios, a dominant actor or driving force may also induce other actors to join through the exercise of physical, political, economic, or institutional coercion, thereby paving the way for a broader convergence of multiple actors. 4. Instruments and Mechanisms for Realizing Hyenaism In a Hyenaistic convergence, participants may coordinate or exploit multiple instruments, including, but not limited to, the following: · Military, political, diplomatic, and economic power; · Consensus-building, agenda-setting, and influencing public opinion at local, national, and international levels; · Mobilization of communities and populations, social constituencies, and organized networks; · Deployment or functional capture of organizations and institutions at local, national, and international levels; · Laws, rules, procedures, regulatory systems, and their selective interpretation; · Cultural narratives, symbols, traditions, and identity frameworks; · Poverty, vulnerability, dependency, or inequalities in access to resources; · Science, technology, information, expertise, and control over knowledge; · Any other capability or resource that can be coordinated in pursuit of a shared objective. The presence of any one of these instruments does not, in itself, imply misconduct. The central question is whether such instruments are collectively and opportunistically employed or exploited to secure a shared advantage at the expense of broader principles, other parties, or the public interest. 5. The Logic of Alliances and Temporary Convergence in Hyenaism Hyenaism describes a form of instrumental alignment: when a common goal, opportunity, or interest comes to the fore, previous hostilities may be temporarily suspended. This does not necessarily imply that fundamental disagreements have been resolved. Cooperation may be tactical, selective, covert, or overt, while competition continues in other domains. 6. Life Cycle and Conditions for the Termination of Hyenaism The life cycle of Hyenaism depends primarily on two interrelated conditions: first, the continuation of shared interests or objectives among the participants; and second, the expected benefit remaining above each participant’s threshold of acceptability, as determined by its cost–benefit considerations or economic, political, or cultural viability. Such convergence may weaken or dissolve when the common opportunity disappears, costs increase, benefits are distributed unequally, risks intensify, or participants’ objectives diverge. If the underlying incentive structure changes, the convergence may transform into a different type of coalition, with a smaller or otherwise different membership than the original group. Thus, Hyenaism is not a permanent organization, but rather a conditional and potentially terminable pattern of alignment. 7. Key Characteristics Instrumental Convergence: The primary driver of cooperation is an expected benefit or the reduction of a perceived threat. Multilevel Scope: The actors involved may be individuals, groups, political parties, countries, or institutions operating at any scale. Diversity of Objectives: Shared interests may be material, non-material, or a combination of both. Multi-Instrument Coordination: Various sources of power and influence may be deployed in a coordinated manner. Conditional Continuity: The survival of the convergence depends on shared interests and the continued acceptability of the net benefit to its participants. External Ethical and Institutional Consequences: The pursuit of shared benefits typically imposes costs on others, the public interest, established rules, or broader principles. 8. Distinction from Conventional Cooperation Not every alliance, compromise, or form of cooperation between rivals can be described as Hyenaism. Conventional cooperation may be transparent, principled, accountable, and directed toward a legitimate public good. items.title: ICoder-27B: Recursive AI-Led Development of Frontier Industrial Coding Model
items.abstract: Recursive AI, the prospect of artificial intelligence taking an increasingly complete role in building and improving artificial intelligence, has so far been demonstrated mostly on small models, bounded tasks, and fixed time budgets. A recent technical report by Yang and colleagues [1] asks a more demanding question: how little human involvement is sufficient for an agent to lead the development of a release-ready, frontier-competitive model? Their answer is an agent-led pipeline that produced iCoder-27B, a 27-billion-parameter model for register-transfer-level (RTL) hardware design and GPU kernel optimization. This paper is an independent technical review and analysis of that report; it does not present new training results.We reconstruct the design principle of high-density human priors with low-frequency intervention, the executable research skills that carry those priors, and the four-stage pipeline of data evolution, supervised fine-tuning, on-policy self-distillation, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards....

items.title: Identification of letters distorted by physiologically-inspired spatial scrambling
items.abstract: In the geniculostriate pathway of the human visual system, neuronal projections carry signals from a particular retinal locus in parallel from one anatomical area to the next. Imprecision in the fidelity of these projections would place constraints on the ability of the system to perform tasks requiring positional information. We investigated the impact that "spatial scrambling" between stages would have on visual performance. We consider two stages in a simple canonical model of the early visual cortex where scrambling might occur: either the input to the first orientation-tuned mechanisms (analogous to V1 simple cells), or the output from those mechanisms. These are referred as "subcortical" (SCS) and "cortical scrambling" (CS). We developed a wavelet decomposition and resynthesis algorithm to mimic these effects, and measured human performance in letter identification affected by the two types of scrambling. Our results showed SCS and CS have distinguishable effects on both perceived noisiness of letters and letter identification threshold. Comparing human performance against a suite of pre-trained and custom convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that were trained on the scrambled stimuli, relative efficiency (calculated from the ratio of human:CNN thresholds) is higher for CS than SCS. However, in modelling human inefficiency by reducing the proportion of wavelets available to the CNNs, humans are less efficient in CS than SCS. These differences in efficiencies show humans are better at processing orientation redundant stimuli (CS) than orientation noisy stimuli (SCS). We hypothesize this reflects differences in integration properties at the input and output stages of simple cells in the cortex.

items.title: Identifying a dynamic information trading zone framework via insights from full-scale emergency exercises
items.abstract: The article examines how the co-creation of a Common Operational Picture (COP) in multi-actor crisis response operations can be understood through the concept of Information Trading Zones (ITZ). The analysis is grounded in the theory of Situation Awareness (SA), including Endsley’s conceptualisation of individual, Team SA and Shared SA, and draws on Galison’s notion of trading zones as intercalation, the insertion of an intermediate concept or mechanism to bridge existing explanatory levels. In this study, ITZ is introduced as an intercalating construct linking information exchange, sensemaking, and coordinated action. Drawing on extensive qualitative analyses of five full-scale crisis exercises, the study traces the evolution of an operational framework that conceptualises ITZ as both a precondition for and an integral component of the co-creation of a COP. Within this framework, ITZ are positioned as socio-technical spaces where information is negotiated, interpreted, and stabilised across organisational boundaries, enabling the development of Shared and Team SA in the face of uncertainty. The article offers concrete recommendations for both researchers and practice, outlining how the interplay among ITZ, COP, and SA can inform the design of information systems that more effectively support coordination, sense-making, and decision-making in Emergency Management contexts.

items.title: Immediate effects of dynamic- and static-based custom insoles on structural alignment, pressure distribution and subjective comfort in paediatric flexible flatfoot
items.abstract: Background Customised insoles for paediatric flexible flatfoot are typically designed using static foot postures, which may fail to reflect the dynamic mechanical demands of gait. This study explored an alternative method, evaluating whether dynamically modelled insoles, captured during active locomotion, can effectively provide optimized kinematic control and plantar load distribution while maintaining ergonomic comfort as compared to traditional static designs. Methods Two insoles were customised for 15 children (8–10 years) with flexible flatfeet: a static-based insole (SI), modelled during seated great toe dorsiflexion, and a dynamic-based insole (DI), modelled from the active arch profile during walking. Assessments included geometric characteristics (arch height and medial longitudinal arch [MLA] angle), rearfoot angle (RFA), peak plantar pressure (PPP), and subjective ergonomic comfort. Results DI exhibited a significantly greater arch height and MLA angle than SI. Kinematically, both designs reduced severe RFA misalignments, with DI demonstrating more consistent bilateral kinematic control. Kinetically, both functioned as effective total-contact devices, attenuating pressure peaks at the heel and lateral forefoot. Notably, despite the more pronounced structural contour of DI, participants reported high subjective comfort scores that were statistically equivalent to SI. Conclusion Both SI and DI effectively improved rearfoot eversion and reduced localized pressures without compromising subjective comfort. Specifically, the dynamic approach achieved greater total-contact load redistribution across the MLA.

items.title: Immersive reality training for oral and maxillofacial microvascular reconstruction in resource-limited settings
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction Microvascular free flap transfer is essential in contemporary oral and maxillofacial reconstruction. However, acquiring microvascular anastomosis skills remains challenging in low-resource settings due to a heavy dependence on high-cost instruments and expert supervision. This scoping review (ScR) mapped the existing evidence on immersive reality (IR) technologies for microvascular anastomosis training and explored their potential applications in educationally limited and low-resource environments. Main body Comprehensive literature searches were performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus for studies published between 2010 and April 2026, following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Seven studies published between 2010 and 2024 met the inclusion criteria. Although these studies supported specific microsurgical tasks, most described proof-of-concept prototypes with limited validation. Furthermore, none evaluated a structured microvascular reconstruction curriculum. Crucially, no included study directly evaluated maxillofacial reconstructive surgeons or trainees, nor did any specifically address head and neck microvascular anastomosis curricula. Conclusion Current evidence indicates technical promise alongside significant literature gaps, as effectiveness, clinical transfer to the operating room, and cost-effectiveness remain unproven. To address training disparities, we introduce an author-proposed staged curriculum framework wherein lower-cost IR platforms provide foundational orientation, instrument handling, depth perception, suture sequencing, and ergonomic visualization before trainees’ progress to bench, biological, and supervised clinical training.

items.title: Implementation of a single-port robotic platform into your colorectal surgery practice: a SAGES colorectal committee task force review of evolving robotic technology and innovations
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Robotic and endoscopic techniques continue to revolutionize minimally invasive surgery. Single-port (SP) robotic platforms mark a new era in minimally invasive colorectal surgery, combining single-incision/site access with full robotic articulation through a single access point. This manuscript, as a part of a four-part series, outlines specific technical considerations of the SP robotic platform including details of the platform, instrumentation, docking, and operative maneuvers. METHODS: Subject matter experts from the SAGES Colorectal Committee SP Task Force performed a structured review of the currently FDA-approved SP robotic platform, assessing technical features, instrumentation, and workflow considerations for several key representative operations relevant to colorectal surgery. Three clinical areas of SP implementation included transanal robotic surgery, right colectomy, and low anterior resection (LAR). Task Force members (subject matter experts with early experience in SP robotic platforms) analyzed technical details, patient selection, and operative workflows. Representative procedural techniques were detailed with emphasis on instrumentation choice, docking strategies, and key operative steps specific to single-port colorectal surgery. RESULTS: The technical aspects of the SP platform include full robotic articulation through a single 25 mm port. A SP approach also enables triangulation and dexterity within confined spaces using three wristed instruments and a flexible 3-D camera. The current 360-degree boom rotation facilitates multi-quadrant manipulation without redocking. Current limitations may include continued reliance on bedside assistance for certain energy and stapling operative steps, although stapling capability has expanded with FDA clearance of an SP-compatible 45 mm stapler as of April 2025. Training of the entire operative team and gradual progression of case complexity is recommended as the surgeon implements this new technology into clinical practice. CONCLUSIONS: A SP robotic approach to minimally invasive colorectal surgical procedures is feasible for a range of colorectal surgery operations. In select procedures like SP TAMIS, SP right colectomy, and SP-LAR, the single-port platform appears to offer advantages related to reduced invasiveness and improved surgeon ergonomics compared to other minimally invasive approaches. Successful implementation requires structured training, careful patient selection, and adherence to evidence-based adoption principles.

items.title: Independent Convergence: MIT, AI, and the Future of Higher Education
items.abstract: This research note compares the January 2026 HEI 2030 Manifesto (Simpson, 2026) with MIT’s August 2026 report on AI in teaching, learning, and research training. It finds substantial independent convergence around a structural diagnosis: AI weakens the relationship between student output and demonstrated capability, requiring assessment redesign, observable performance, stronger human agency, and continuous institutional governance. The January manifesto goes further in specifying an integrated operating model linking assessment, task-level governance, credential signaling, and human-AI work. MIT develops community, mentoring, privacy, access, and implementation resources more fully. The comparison then raises a harder question: whether credible AI-era education is economically scalable overall.

items.title: Innovations in higher education: a methodology for the integration of artificial intelligence and pedagogical technologies
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence technologies, particularly generative AI and chatbots, into higher education necessitates a fundamental reconceptualization of the relationship between technological capabilities and pedagogical approaches. This article presents a comprehensive methodology for integrating artificial intelligence and pedagogical technologies (digital pedagogy) into the higher education system, with a specific emphasis on content verification as a critical component for reliable AI implementation. The methodological foundations of this comprehensive methodology are based on research in the fields of educational data mining, predictive analytics, and recommender systems conducted between 2019 and 2025, providing a robust theoretical and empirical basis for the proposed methodological integration. This study synthesizes scientific developments in technical, psychological, and pedagogical research to address the challenge of ensuring the authenticity of educational content while simultaneously developing students’ critical thinking skills. The proposed methodology encompasses a conceptual framework for AI and digital pedagogy integration, a data storage architecture, algorithms for data collection and preprocessing, verification protocols for generated content, and pedagogical strategies for using verification as a learning tool. The practical significance of this research lies in the development of content verification tools and methodological guidelines for the use of AI in higher education institutions.

items.title: Installation Personas: A Persona-Centered Framework for AI-Driven Interactive Art Installations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is enabling interactive art installations to become increasingly adaptive and socially interactive, yet limited conceptual guidance exists for analyzing installations themselves as persona-like entities. In this study, the Installation Persona Framework is proposed, extending persona-centered analysis from users and individual AI agents to AI-driven interactive installations. The framework conceptualizes Persona Identity through two complementary dimensions—Persona Type and Persona Role—and examines their expression through Persona Behavior and Interaction and association with Artistic Function and Intended Audience Experience. Using a structured screening process, 41 AI-driven interactive installations were selected from 329 artworks presented at the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) AI Art Gallery from 2024 to 2026. Qualitative analysis identified seven recurring Persona Archetypes and eight higher-order Persona Role Families. An independent classification assessment carried out by four external coders showed statistically significant but fair intercoder agreement for Persona Archetype (Fleiss’ κ = 0.266) and Persona Role Family (κ = 0.203), indicating measurable but limited classification reproducibility and ambiguity in category boundaries. Because audience evaluation was not conducted, audience experience was limited to artist-intended or researcher-inferred interpretations based on available documentation. Overall, the framework provides a structured vocabulary for analyzing AI-driven interactive installations as integrated persona-like entities.

items.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence in Journalism Education: Curricular Gaps and Educator Perspectives From Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming journalism and creating challenges for journalism education. Guided by Diffusion of Innovations theory, this study examines AI integration in journalism education in Bangladesh. Using a qualitative multi-method design, the study analyzed 21 curricula from 17 universities and interviewed 18 journalism educators, including 12 faculty members and 6 department heads. Findings reveal limited formal AI integration despite educators’ recognition of its professional importance, reflecting a gap between individual recognition and institutional adoption shaped by infrastructure, expertise, funding, and policy constraints. The study highlights the need for context-sensitive curriculum reform, sustained faculty development, and practical AI training.

items.title: Integrating Human Resource Analytics into Business Education Curriculum: Perspectives of Senior Human Resource Managers in Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study investigated integrating human resource analytics into the postgraduate Business Education curriculum: Perspectives of senior human resource managers in Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria. It became imperative due to the widening gap between traditional, theory-based business pedagogy and the data-driven workforce requirements of modern corporate organisations. The descriptive survey research design was adopted. The study sampled 120 senior HR managers from key economic sectors using purposive and convenience sampling methods. Data were gathered via “Human Resource Analytics Integration in Business Education Questionnaire (HRALBEQ)”, validated by HRM and Measurement and Evaluation experts, pilot-tested, and confirmed using the Cronbach’s alpha method, which yielded a reliability coefficient of 0.88. Data were analysed using mean scores and standard deviation for the research questions, and an independent t-test was used to test null hypotheses at .05 level of significance. The findings of the study revealed a critical, great extent demand from HR managers to include descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics (advanced data literacy) in the Business Education curriculum. Notably, both public and private sector managers shared identical views, providing educational policymakers with a clear road map to update the curriculum. Based on these findings, it was recommended that universities in Nigeria should establish modern, data-driven Business Education laboratories to train postgraduate students in descriptive HR metrics, enabling them to systematically collect, clean, and visualise fundamental workforce data using industry-standard tools like Power Business Intelligence and Excel. It was also recommended that tertiary institutions in the state should introduce predictive modeling for talent forecasting, and prescriptive analytics through corporate workplace learning projects.

items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), such as GPT, BERT, RoBERTa, and their variants, have significantly transformed the traditional natural language processing (NLP) by providing rich context-sensitive representation and offering sophisticated generative capabilities. Clustering is a fundamental unsupervised learning approach, primarily organizing unlabelled data, discover latent patterns, employed to perform tasks such as topic modelling, and document classification. The assimilation of these two domains has the capability to enhance representation learning and discovering structure in large, unannotated corpora. This research paper explores the possibility of enhancing clustering results with LLM&s;s embedding and utilizing clustering techniques to LLM outputs for better insights. The paper discusses advancement in methodology, comparative analyses, application context, and challenges. The discussion also highlights the emerging research directions that reveal the scope for embedding clustering techniques in the LLM learning process.

items.title: Interactive and inspectable LLM planning for human-in-the-loop EV battery disassembly
items.abstract: Introduction Intent-driven robotic disassembly requires translating operator language and noisy RGB-D perception into grounded, precedence-consistent removal plans. This work extends a perception-grounded large language model (LLM) planning framework for two-arm electric vehicle (EV) battery disassembly and evaluates the pipeline’s effectiveness after replacing the LLM backbone. Methods The system converts live RGB-D detections into structured scene text, rewrites coordinates into a frame-consistent LUZD representation, generates an ordered removal sequence, validates it with an LLM verifier, and applies a deterministic anti-hallucination filter that removes labels or coordinates not present in the perceived scene. The replacement LLM is first evaluated within the prior ensemble-based pipeline. The upgraded system then combines a single-checkpoint generator-verifier workflow, revised generator and verifier prompts, and an interactive, inspectable human-in-the-loop planning interface that displays intermediate outputs and final filtered plans. Results On the same 200-scene, 600-intent benchmark used in earlier work, mean full-list correctness was 0.824 for the prior six-sample final pipeline, 0.896 when the replacement LLM was evaluated within that prior pipeline, 0.935 with the upgraded generator alone, and 0.959 with verification and filtering. The final upgraded configuration reduced the LLM-call count from seven to two. In a 12-participant within-subject pilot, mean time to accepted answer was lower on both tasks, the mean raw NASA-TLX score was lower, and all participants preferred the new interface. Discussion These results suggest that structured scene text, clear prompts, verifier-based correction, deterministic grounding, and inspectable interfaces enhance human-in-the-loop disassembly planning.

items.title: Internet of Things-Based Physical Security Systems for Smart Cities in Saudi Arabia: A Vision 2030 Framework
items.abstract: The rapid digitalisation of cities in Saudi Arabia is leading to a greater number of connected cameras, access-control devices, environmental sensors, edge gateways and city platforms being used for the protection of people, buildings and critical infrastructure. While these systems can enhance situational awareness, they also turn physical security into a cyber-physical issue in which compromised identities, networks, analytics or actuators can have real-world effects. This review draws on peer-reviewed evidence published between 2020 and 2025 to look at how Internet of Things technologies can support physical security in Saudi smart cities while remaining resilient, privacy-conscious and operationally governable. Thirty studies verified by DOI were examined using a structured integrative approach that included topics such as smart-city security, IoT architectures, video analytics, intrusion detection, distributed trust, federated learning, digital twins, emergency response and Saudi urban governance. The synthesis highlights five interdependent capability areas: trusted sensing, edge intelligence, resilient connectivity, secure city platforms and coordinated response. It concludes that the technical effectiveness of these systems is more a matter of managing device identity, software provenance, data minimisation, model assurance, interoperability and multi-agency operating procedures than of adding more sensors. A framework aligned with Vision 2030 is suggested, focusing on risk-based zoning, zero-trust device governance, privacy-preserving analytics, resilient edge-cloud orchestration, integrated command workflows and lifecycle assurance. The framework views physical security as an adaptive public-service capability rather than as a set of separate surveillance products. The research priorities are Saudi field trials, climate-resilient sensing, common evaluation benchmarks, measuring privacy impacts and carrying out a longitudinal assessment of human-centred security outcomes.

items.title: Intersubjective resilience: Sustaining collective life under persistent life-and-death risk
items.abstract: How do organizations sustain collective life when exposure to life-and-death risk becomes a persistent condition of work? Based on an ethnographic study of two elite police units operating under continuous life-and-death risk, we find that organizations sustain coordinated collective life not by eliminating fear, resolving contradictions, or restoring stability, but by continually reorganizing these pressures into shared forms of action. We identify three interrelated organizing mechanisms. First, aspirational discipline transforms vulnerability into collective moral obligation by aligning individual striving with shared purpose. Second, paradoxical knotting enables members to act through enduring tensions, such as aggression and restraint or autonomy and obedience, without having to resolve them. Third, routine enactment restores coordinated action through recurring practices of training, reflection, and operational work. Together, these mechanisms explain how organizations maintain coherent and coordinated action when danger is an everyday condition of work. We conceptualize this capacity as intersubjective resilience : the collective accomplishment through which members repeatedly transform fear, contradiction, and disruption into coordinated action under persistent life-and-death risk.

items.title: Intrinsic and Organizational Drivers of Civil Servants' Work Motivation in Public Service Delivery: A Documentary Evidence Synthesis from Central Maluku, Indonesia
items.abstract: Civil servants' motivation is central to public-service performance, particularly in geographically dispersed local governments. This study identifies intrinsic motivational mechanisms and organizational conditions relevant to public-service delivery at the Regional Personnel and Human Resources Development Agency (BKPSDM) of Central Maluku, Indonesia. A qualitative documentary case study combined with an integrative evidence synthesis was employed. A final evidence set of 21 sources was organized into four source groups, guided by a documented search logic and eligibility protocol. Deductive and inductive coding were applied, and driver clusters were retained through three independent evidence-stream criteria: broader evidence (A), Indonesian public-sector empirical evidence (B), and direct Central Maluku/BKPSDM relevance (C). The findings show that recurrent intrinsic mechanisms include recognition and achievement, responsibility and autonomy, professional growth and competence, and public-service meaning. Organizational conditions include supervisory and organizational support, goal and administrative clarity, career development and non-financial recognition, workable administrative systems, manageable job demands, supportive working conditions, and service-user feedback. These findings suggest that motivation should be managed through a complementary architecture that links meaningful work and psychological need satisfaction with organizational resources and constraints. The documentary design provides a context-grounded framework for field testing but does not estimate employee-level causal effects.

items.title: Introduction
items.abstract: The study of human performance on a bicycle is not a recent phenomenon. Indeed, the cycle ergometer has been a cornerstone of physiological research for over a century, evolving from the rudimentary friction-braked devices of the late 19th century to the sophisticated laboratory instruments of today ( Vandewalle & Driss, 2015 ). This long history provided the foundation to investigate the fundamental principles of exercise physiology, many of which were first articulated by Nobel laureate A.V. Hill. His pioneering work distinguishing aerobic from anaerobic metabolism and defining concepts such as “maximum O 2 intake” established the theoretical questions that the ergometer was uniquely positioned to answer in the exercising human ( Bassett, 2002 ). The subsequent standardisation and widespread adoption of laboratory ergometry laid the groundwork for an explosion of research. In recent decades, the technological leap from stationary ergometers to mobile, on-bike power meters has coincided with a dramatic growth in scientific publications, rising from 855 in 1985 to over 18,000 in 2024 ( Figure 1.1 ).

items.title: Job rotation: A bibliometric analysis
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Job rotation is a strategic practice aimed at improving employees' health, satisfaction, and overall productivity in organizations. Its ergonomic aspects are crucial because they help balance workload, reduce ergonomic risks, and support an aging workforce. OBJECTIVE: This study addresses the lack of a field-level synthesis of job rotation research by conducting a bibliometric analysis of publications from 1994 through 2025, with particular attention to ergonomic themes, trends, and relationships in the literature. METHODS: A bibliometric analysis was conducted using 820 records retrieved from Scopus. VOSviewer was used to examine keyword co-occurrence, country co-authorship, author bibliographic coupling, title-and-abstract term co-occurrence, and author co-citation networks. RESULTS: The analysis shows rapid growth in the literature on job rotation and its critical components. The visualizations show the evolution of research topics and their interrelationships. The mapped literature emphasizes ergonomic and organizational themes including workload balancing, musculoskeletal risk, work design, scheduling, worker well-being, and job satisfaction. CONCLUSIONS: The study underlines the increasing emphasis on the ergonomic and organizational benefits of job rotation. It proposes conducting further research to address existing gaps and promote employee well-being and productivity through effective job rotation strategies.

items.title: JustOPD: On-Policy Distillation from Autoregressive to Diffusion Language Models
items.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training approach for large language models (LLMs) that enables a student model to learn a teacher model's distribution from sequences sampled from the student's own policy. Despite its promising capability, OPD for diffusion language models (DLMs) remains underexplored and existing studies primarily focuses on DLM-to-DLM distillation. The limited availability of strong teacher DLMs and the flexible generation order of DLMs impose additional technical challenges as well. However, it remains unclear how to effectively distill knowledge from a strong autoregressive language model (ARM) into a weaker DLM, given the mismatch between the left-to-right decoding of ARMs and the flexible decoding order of DLMs. Inspired by Ni et al. (2026), we propose JustOPD, an ARM-to-DLM on-policy distillation method that uses autoregressive rollouts during training to align the student's generation process with the ARM teacher's left-to-right decoding. This alignment enables effective distillation from ARM teachers while preserving the DLM's flexible generation-order capability at inference time. Experiments using Qwen3-14B as the teacher and Dream-7B as the student demonstrate that JustOPD consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance over the base DLM across multiple divergence choices.

items.title: Knowledge Sharing and Organizational Performance: A Systematic Review and Thematic Synthesis of Mechanisms, Contexts and Outcomes (2014-2025)
items.abstract: Purpose: This review explains how knowledge sharing is converted into organizational performance and identifies the organizational, technological and contextual conditions that enable, constrain or redirect this conversion. Design/methodology/approach: A systematic literature review covering 2014-2025 was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 reporting principles and management-review guidance. The final analytical corpus comprises 92 empirical studies: 46 published during 2014-2024 and 46 published in 2025. The 2014-2024 screening sequence reported in the manuscript began with 1,204 records, of which 912 remained after deduplication; 96 were assessed in full text and 46 were retained. For 2025, 75 records were identified; after removal of duplicates/overlaps, one out-of-period record and two retracted reports, 67 were assessed and 46 retained. Eligibility, extraction and thematic coding were conducted by a single primary reviewer using explicit criteria, an audit trail and repeated coding. The synthesis combined descriptive mapping with iterative thematic analysis; no meta-analysis was conducted because constructs, outcome levels and effect statistics were heterogeneous. Findings: Across the 2014-2025 literature, five interdependent themes emerged: enabling and inhibiting conditions; forms and quality of knowledge sharing; conversion mechanisms; multidimensional performance outcomes; and boundary conditions. The evidence is consistent with a conditional conversion pathway in which culture, trust, leadership, support, structure and digital infrastructure shape exchange, while learning, innovation, improvisation, agility, ambidexterity, knowledge quality and application help explain how sharing is associated with performance. The 2025 subset places stronger emphasis on artificial intelligence, human-machine interaction, knowledge-sharing quality, sustainability and the balance between sharing and protection. This late-period concentration is interpreted as an emerging development rather than a definitive temporal break. Mixed and non-significant findings show that more sharing is not automatically better. Research limitations/implications: The evidence remains dominated by cross-sectional, self-reported SEM studies and emerging-economy contexts. A single-reviewer process and heterogeneous outcome measures limit causal and statistical generalization. Practical implications: Managers should manage the complete conversion chain: identify strategically relevant knowledge, create safe and well-governed sharing channels, validate quality, embed application in work processes and evaluate proximal and distal performance outcomes. Originality/value: The review extends earlier enabler-process-outcome syntheses by isolating the knowledge-sharing-to-performance pathway, separating proximal from distal performance outcomes, incorporating boundary conditions and failure paths, and proposing a dynamic conversion framework that integrates AI, knowledge quality, ambidexterity and governance. It also distinguishes established themes across the review period from emerging emphases concentrated in the 2025 subset.

items.title: L'audit financier à l'ère de l'intelligence artificielle au Maroc : enjeux éthiques, transparence algorithmique et responsabilité professionnelle
items.abstract: Résumé L’intelligence artificielle transforme les modalités de collecte, de traitement et d’interprétation des éléments probants en audit financier. Les outils d’apprentissage automatique, d’analyse de données et de traitement du langage permettent d’élargir la couverture des tests, d’automatiser certaines procédures et de repérer plus rapidement les opérations atypiques. Leur performance ne garantit toutefois pas, à elle seule, la qualité de l’audit. Les biais issus des données, l’opacité des modèles, la dépendance technologique, la confidentialité et la dilution des responsabilités peuvent fragiliser le jugement professionnel. Cet article théorique analyse la manière dont l’intégration de l’IA reconfigure les exigences d’éthique, de transparence et de responsabilité dans l’audit financier au Maroc. La recherche adopte une démarche qualitative fondée sur une revue narrative structurée de la littérature académique, des normes internationales et du cadre institutionnel marocain. La théorie des systèmes socio-techniques est mobilisée pour expliquer que la qualité de l’audit dépend de l’ajustement entre technologies, compétences, procédures et gouvernance. L’analyse conduit à un modèle reliant l’usage raisonné de l’IA à la qualité de l’audit et à la confiance des parties prenantes, sous l’effet de la qualité des données, de l’explicabilité, de la supervision humaine et des compétences. Sept propositions de recherche et un cadre d’encadrement en sept piliers sont formulés. L’article montre que la responsabilité finale demeure humaine et que la technologie ne peut fournir une assurance crédible que si ses résultats sont traçables, contestables et replacés dans le contexte de la mission. La contribution réside dans l’intégration des dimensions techniques, cognitives et institutionnelles au sein d’un cadre adapté au contexte marocain. Mots clés : intelligence artificielle ; audit financier ; éthique professionnelle ; transparence algorithmique ; explicabilité ; responsabilité ; Maroc. Abstract Artificial intelligence is transforming how audit evidence is collected, processed and interpreted. Machine learning, data analytics and natural language processing can extend testing coverage, automate selected procedures and identify unusual transactions more rapidly. Yet technical performance does not, by itself, ensure audit quality. Data-related bias, model opacity, technological dependence, confidentiality risks and fragmented accountability may weaken professional judgment. This conceptual article examines how artificial intelligence reshapes ethical requirements, algorithmic transparency and professional responsibility in financial auditing in Morocco. The study adopts a qualitative approach based on a structured narrative review of academic research, international professional standards and the Moroccan institutional framework. Socio-technical systems theory is used to explain why audit quality depends on the joint alignment of technologies, skills, procedures and governance arrangements. The analysis develops a model linking the reasoned use of artificial intelligence to audit quality and stakeholder trust, subject to data quality, explainability, meaningful human oversight and professional competencies. Seven research propositions and a seven-pillar governance framework are formulated. The article argues that final accountability remains human and that technology can contribute to credible assurance only when its outputs are traceable, contestable and interpreted within the engagement context. Its contribution lies in integrating technical, cognitive and institutional dimensions into a framework suited to the Moroccan environment and capable of guiding future empirical research. Keywords: artificial intelligence; financial auditing; professional ethics; algorithmic transparency; explainability; accountability; Morocco.

items.title: Label Collapse in Diffusion Language Model In-Context Learning
items.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) applies large language models to new tasks by prepending a few labeled demonstrations to a query. Prior work has studied how demonstration ordering affects ICL, but the interaction between label arrangement patterns and model biases has not been systematically examined. We define label collapse as the failure mode in which the model generates query-independent labels, and show that it is architecturally universal at the tested 8-9B scale: five models spanning autoregressive (Llama-3, Qwen3.5) and discrete diffusion (LLaDA, iLLaDA, LLaDA-Instruct) families all exhibit label collapse even under the class-balanced alternating arrangement, with some label word pairs collapsing in virtually every tested condition and others flipping their collapse direction with arrangement. Critically, accuracy alone cannot detect this collapse: models can achieve near-chance accuracy while generating query-independent labels, a score indistinguishable from balanced performance, so the failure can persist undetected in deployment. We measure separation, the log-odds of the two label words at the query position (the quantity that label-bias calibration operates on), as a complementary diagnostic that exposes collapse hidden beneath surface accuracy, together with a measurement protocol that guards label extraction against tokenizer and formatting artifacts. For autoregressive models, collapse persists where the majority-label-bias account does not apply, and arrangement patterns can reverse the collapse direction; for diffusion models, we present a systematic evaluation of ICL failure modes, complementing contemporaneous studies of dLLM context comprehension and demonstration-order sensitivity, and identify open questions about how iterative denoising interacts with label biases.

items.abstract: Stroke is major wellbeing condition which creates serious hazard to human health and cause of bereavement and disability universal. Several risk factors contribute to its development, including hypertension, diabetes, tobacco use, raised cholesterol levels, and obesity. Conventional methods have been used to predict stroke, however it frequently face demands in achieving enhanced accuracy as well as minimizing errors. Initially, patient data samples are gathered from relevant datasets during the data acquisition stage. Input information is first transferred to input level, then forwarded to first hidden layer, where pre-processing takes place. This includes handling missing values through Multiple Imputations by Chained Equations (MICE) technique and removing anomalies or outliers using High Contrast Subspace method to compromise model performance. In second hidden level, is executed by Laplace Copula Multivariate feature ranking method, which identifies and retains the most relevant features. Subsequently, the third hidden layer handles the stroke prediction phase by employing Logistic Regression as a binary classification model to accurately forecast the presence or absence of stroke based on a selected set of relevant features. A probability is then used to classify the patient as either stroke or not. To optimize model performance during training, error backpropagation is employed for weight adjustment, and hyperparameters are fine-tuned using the Adaptive Moment Estimation optimizer. Experimental assessment of LACO-GAI model is conducted using various assessment parameters. Quantitatively examined outcomes expose LACO-GAI obtains superior accuracy in stroke disease prediction by lesser time consumption compared to DL techniques.

items.title: Large Language Model Assisted Transportation Planning through a Differentiable User Equilibrium Layer
items.abstract: Transportation planning has traditionally required substantial expertise in network modeling, traffic assignment, and optimization. As a result, strategic analyses such as network design, capacity expansion, and model calibration remain inaccessible to non-expert decision makers. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to bridge this gap by enabling natural-language interaction with complex transportation planning tools. However, existing LLM-based systems primarily serve as interfaces to simulation software and lack the ability to efficiently search, evaluate, and optimize transportation solutions. This study proposes an integrated human-AI transportation planning framework that combines a large language model, a model context protocol (MCP) interface, an open-source transportation planning engine (AequilibraE), and a differentiable user equilibrium (UE) assignment layer. The framework allows non-expert users to execute network analyses and improve solutions for optimization. A differentiable UE layer is developed by directly differentiating the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions of the Beckmann traffic assignment problem. The proposed framework is demonstrated through two representative planning tasks: calibration of travel time functions from observed traffic counts and network design under budget constraints. The examples illustrate how differentiable transportation models and LLM agents can jointly democratize transportation planning and substantially reduce barriers between domain expertise and transportation decision making.

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into materials discovery is hindered by the trade‐off between exploration breadth and exploitation depth, while the lack of embedded domain knowledge and systematic chemical space compression further limits intelligent materials exploration under data scarcity. Herein, we propose a literature‐knowledge‐directed iterative workflow that combines large language models (LLMs) with Bayesian optimization (BO) for the rational electrolyte design for ultra‐stable sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs). LLMs serve as auxiliary tools for knowledge mining, while BO accelerates multi‐objective optimization to obtain electrolyte compositions. The optimized dual‐anion hybrid solvation electrolyte (DHSE) constructs a synergistic solvation structure, which induces the formation of a compact, inorganic‐rich, and mechanically robust cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI). The as‐formed CEI layer suppresses parasitic side reactions and accelerates Na + transport by reducing the desolvation barrier. Remarkably, industrial‐scale Ah‐level hard carbon||NaNi 0.3 Mn 0.3 Fe 0.3 O 2 pouch cells assembled with DHSE deliver a high energy density of 107.7 Wh kg −1 , alongside a superior capacity retention of 94% after 100 cycles at 0.5C. This work not only develops a high‐performance electrolyte for practically applicable SIBs but also provides a general human‐agent collaborative framework for intelligent materials development under data‐limited conditions.

items.title: Large Language Models Extend Known Research But Do Not Create New Research Directions
items.abstract: The success of autonomous research systems relies on the quality of the scientific hypotheses they generate. Recent studies report that human reviewers often rate LLM-generated ideas as more novel than those from human experts, raising hope that AI can accelerate scientific discovery. Yet it is unclear whether these models can do more than extend existing knowledge. Can LLMs drive genuine innovation by revealing new research directions, or are they limited to repeating and recombining what science already knows? This unresolved question lies at the heart of discussions about AI and the future of science. To address this, we distinguish two types of novelty: distance, which measures how far a hypothesis lies from existing work, and direction, which captures whether the hypothesis pursues new lines of inquiry beyond those already present. These two measures diverge sharply for LLM-generated work. We represent scientific papers in a shared conceptual space using a pretrained scientific-paper embedding model. Within this space, we embed 26.9 million human-authored papers across 1,325 research topics in six natural-science fields and 524,308 LLM-generated hypotheses from eight models. Distance is measured using existing metrics. To quantify direction, we introduce the orthogonal novelty score (ONS). LLMs consistently generate ideas more distant from existing work than human-authored papers, up to 16\% further when the LLM is given the papers farthest from the centre of the topic. However, LLM hypotheses have a 15--23\% lower median ONS than published papers from the same topic. Thus, LLMs move further from what is already known, but remain within established directions. This pattern persists across changes in various configurations. As a result, LLMs excel at extending the frontier but the creation of new directions is still led by human scientists.

items.title: Large Language Models for Cybersecurity in the Quantum Era: A Critical Review of Trustworthy AI, Emerging Threats, and Post-Quantum Defense
items.abstract: The convergence of two disruptive forces — large-scale foundation models (large languagemodels, LLMs, and multimodal systems) and the maturing threat of quantum computing — is reshaping cybersecurityfrom both the defensive and offensive sides. Large models are being embedded into security operations, vulnerabilitydiscovery, and threat-intelligence pipelines, while quantum algorithms threaten to invalidate the public-key infrastructureunderlying nearly all deployed cryptographic protocols. Despite an explosion of publications in both areas, the literatureremains fragmented: AI-for-security research rarely engages with post-quantum considerations, and post-quantumcryptography (PQC) research rarely engages with the trustworthiness failures of the AI systems that will manage themigration. Methods. This paper conducts a critical, structured review synthesizing evidence from AI security, systemssecurity, and post-quantum cryptography literature published primarily between 2020 and 2026. We construct a multidimensional taxonomy of AI-for-cybersecurity paradigms, systematize large-model-specific trustworthiness failures —adversarial robustness, data poisoning, prompt injection, model extraction, hallucination, and supply-chain risk — andmap the intersection between AI-enabled defense and AI-assisted post-quantum migration. Key findings. Reportedperformance gains for LLM-based security tools are frequently measured on narrow, contamination-prone benchmarksthat do not reflect adversarial, non-stationary production environments. Prompt injection remains structurally unsolvedrather than merely under-mitigated: reported task-hijacking success rates against tool-using agents rise sharply onceattackers tailor techniques to agent-specific behavior. Offensive robustness evaluation lags defensive-capability evaluationby roughly an order of magnitude in surveyed agentic-security papers. AI-assisted tooling for PQC migration —cryptographic discovery, code auditing, risk scoring — is nascent and inherits the reliability problems of the underlyingmodels it is built on. Implications. We argue the two challenges are entangled rather than parallel: securing the migrationto quantum-resistant cryptography will depend on AI-assisted automation at a scale classical tooling cannot match, yetthat automation must be trusted under exactly the adversarial conditions where current large models are weakest. Weclose with a prioritized research agenda spanning evaluation methodology, quantum-aware threat modeling, and cryptoagility tooling for 2026–2035.Index Terms—artificial intelligence; cybersecurity; large language models; adversarial machine learning; promptinjection; post-quantum cryptography; quantum computing; trustworthy AI; security operations; AI red teaming

items.title: Learning Perceptual Geometry of Natural Odor Mixtures from LLM-Derived Descriptors
items.abstract: The relationship between odor chemistry and perception remains incompletely understood. Many existing studies focus on the perception of single molecules, whereas natural odors contain tens to hundreds of components, adding extra layer of complexity to percept formation. Here, we explore the relationship between molecular composition and perceived similarity in natural odor objects. We study this using a database of more than 1,200 volatile-compound-in-food mixtures containing more than 8,000 molecular components, and use large language models (LLMs) as a scalable surrogate for deriving mixture-level perceptual descriptions. We find that language-derived representations provide useful supervision for predicting held-out mixture similarities from molecular composition. The prediction was consistently strongest when perceptual targets were derived from chemosensory prompts than from other sensory prompts. Further, during the mixture-level training, we learned low-rank molecular embeddings that enabled better prediction of held-out mixture similarities than component-overlap metrics, even for mixture pairs with no shared molecules. Although no single-molecule labels were used during training, the learned molecular geometry showed significant alignment with the independent human odor-descriptor space. Finally, we explored the use of external molecular features in our mixture-similarity prediction task. These features showed modest zero-shot alignment with mixture-level perceptual similarity. They improved prediction under limited supervision but offered little additional predictive benefit with the full training set. Together, these results show that language-derived descriptions can provide scalable supervision for predicting the perceptual organization of complex natural mixtures, contributing to a quantitative understanding of how molecular composition gives rise to odor perception.

items.title: Learning Temporal Evidence Selection for Video Anomaly Understanding
items.abstract: Video anomaly understanding (VAU) aims to generate language-level interpretations of anomalous events in long videos, requiring visual evidence that supports explanation beyond anomaly detection alone. Existing VAU pipelines commonly rely on anomaly-centric or predefined temporal sampling strategies, which efficiently emphasize suspicious moments but overlook contextual cues, object interactions, and temporally distributed evidence needed for reasoning. Motivated by recent progress in learnable temporal selection for long-video question answering, we revisit VAU temporal sampling as a downstream-aligned evidence selection problem. We introduce the semantic-conditioned Temporal Sampling Q-Former that learns to select temporal visual evidence through the VAU generation objective. Since generic VAU prompts provide weak video-specific guidance, we condition the sampler on CLIP-embedded object tags automatically extracted from the input video. These tags are used only for temporal evidence selection and are not appended to the LLM generation prompt, separating sampler conditioning from prompt augmentation. The proposed sampler operates in visual-token space, computes soft temporal selection weights from frame-level representations, and merges duplicated selections before response generation. Experiments on HIVAU-70K show that our model achieves the best performance among the compared fine-tuned models, while ablations demonstrate that learnable temporal sampling improves over fixed anomaly-focused sampling and that CLIP-embedded object-tag conditioning further improves over generic-prompt conditioning. Our results suggest that temporal sampling in VAU should be aligned with explanation-oriented evidence utility rather than anomaly saliency alone.

items.title: Learning to Design SR Solvers: Harness Optimization for Symbolic Regression
items.abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) seeks explicit equations that explain observed data, and recent methods increasingly employ large language models (LLMs) and agents for equation discovery. However, these systems typically rely on manually designed workflows and prompts. We argue that the SR agent harness should itself be an optimization target: its design shapes search priors and how numerical feedback guides subsequent equation refinement. We therefore propose HarnessSR, a framework for jointly optimizing prompts and workflows to construct reusable SR agents. During both harness optimization and agent execution, HarnessSR supports either PySR or an LLM-based equation generator through tool-specific interfaces, allowing the framework to optimize search guidance for different equation-discovery mechanisms. HarnessSR first optimizes role prompts through equation-discovery feedback in basic workflows, then jointly searches prompt assignments and workflows with brief adaptation to align the two. Finally, it refines role instructions through reflection on residual patterns, candidate equation structures, and search outcomes, improving how these signals guide subsequent equation search. On LSR-Synth in LLM-SRBench, HarnessSR achieves a mean ID $\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01}$ of 61.33% across three backbones, a 45.0% relative improvement over the next-best baseline.

items.title: Learning to Detect Shifts in Unstructured Data Streams via Monitoring-by-Betting
items.abstract: Continuous monitoring of generative AI systems requires detecting distribution shifts in the unstructured data they ingest and generate. Existing monitoring methods typically control false alarms by requiring the discrepancy measure used to detect shifts to be *pre-specified*. However, for unstructured data, pre-specification creates a sensitivity--breadth trade-off: a narrowly defined measure is sensitive to the anticipated shift but may miss unexpected changes, whereas a broadly defined measure may detect a wider range of shifts but with reduced sensitivity. Although adaptively hypothesizing the shift direction can overcome this limitation, such data-dependent adaptation generally invalidates conventional false-alarm guarantees. We reconcile adaptivity with statistical validity through testing-by-betting, reframing sequential changepoint detection as a betting game in which the bettor continually updates its hypothesized shift direction, or witness function, as new observations arrive. We introduce *asymptotic e-detectors*, which approximate the pre-change distribution using a calibration set of size $m$, and prove that they asymptotically control the average run length to a false alarm as $m$ increases. Empirically, calibration sets as small as $m=30$ provide effective control. We then develop adaptive monitoring strategies ranging from black-box bettors that learn from embeddings to interpretable bettors based on LLM-proposed concepts. Across three real-world datasets, including data from a clinical AI scribe deployment, adaptive monitors detect shifts faster than fixed monitors at the same false-alarm level. Further, when the true shifts are sparse and interpretable, LLM-concept monitors provide the fastest and most interpretable detection, while also guiding root-cause diagnosis for complex shifts.

items.title: Learning to GUIDE the Group: Self-Learning LLM Facilitation Across Multi-Party Tasks
items.abstract: As large language models are increasingly adopted as multi-party communication facilitators, there is a growing demand for agents capable of balancing diverse group dynamics across contexts. However, existing LLM facilitators are often fine-tuned for task-specific objectives; generalized LLM-based facilitation methods that can adapt to different types of tasks and diverse group dynamics are underdeveloped. To address this gap, we present GUIDE (Generalized Unified Intervention for Dynamic Exchanges, a framework for developing generalized LLM-based facilitators across different multi-party contexts. GUIDE evaluates facilitation across both objective task outcomes and subjective metrics, including psychological safety and perceived friction. Within this framework, we study whether LLMs can self-learn generalized facilitation strategy offline to real-time interventions. We first collect multi-party human interactions guided by task-specific expert LLM facilitators (N=432 conversations). We then employ a self-learning method in which an LLM induces an actionable strategic playbook from conversations and iteratively refines it using feedback from an LLM judge aligned with human annotators (N=20), developing a single generalized facilitator that outperforms the three task-specific expert facilitators on held-out conversations 61.4% win rate. Finally, we evaluate these improvements empirically; in a real-time online empirical study, the self-learned generalized facilitator preserves facilitator performance and group productivity, improves speaking comfort and reduces interpersonal friction, while using 24.7% fewer turns and 29.0% fewer words than the expert prompts. These findings provide empirical evidence that LLMs can learn generalizable, task-agnostic social facilitation from task-specific human interactions, on-par with hand-crafted task-specific prompts across diverse group settings.

items.title: Learning to Play: Reinforcement Learning and Games
items.abstract: Amazing breakthroughs in reinforcement learning have taken place. Computers teach themselves to play Chess and Go and beat world champions. There is talk about expanding application areas towards general artificial intelligence (AI). The breakthroughs in Backgammon, Checkers, Chess, Atari, Go, Poker, and StarCraft have shown that we can build machines that exhibit intelligent game playing of the highest level. These successes have been widely publicized in the media, and inspire AI entrepreneurs and scientists alike. Reinforcement learning in games has become a mainstream AI research topic. It is a broad topic, and the successes build on a range of diverse techniques, from exact planning algorithms, to adaptive sampling, deep function approximation, and ingenious self-play methods. Perhaps because of the breadth of these technologies, or because of the recency of the breakthroughs, there are few books that explain these methods in depth. This book covers all methods in one comprehensive volume, explaining the latest research, bringing you as close as possible to working implementations, with many references to the original research papers. The programming examples in this book are in Python, the language in which most current reinforcement learning research is conducted. We help you to get started with machine learning frameworks such as Gym, TensorFlow, and Keras, and provide exercises to help understand how AI is learning to play.

items.abstract: Abstract:This research monograph provides a rigorous comparative legal and corporate governance analysis of data procurement in frontier generative artificial intelligence development. Focusing on the normative divergence between Article 30-4 of the Japanese Copyright Act and the Fair Use doctrine under 17 U.S.C. §107, we examine cross-border conflicts of law arising when data extraction, compute training, and model serving occur in separate jurisdictions. Furthermore, the paper analyzes the liability allocation between AI developers and compute/cloud infrastructure providers, distinguishing passive IaaS/PaaS conduits from integrated strategic partnerships. Grounded in Delaware corporate governance standards (the Caremark doctrine) and ESG supply-chain due diligence, we establish a practical compliance and contractual risk-allocation architecture to ensure sustainable, transparent knowledge ecosystems.

items.title: Less can be more for predicting properties with large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Predicting properties from coordinate–category data—sets of vectors paired with categorical information—is fundamental to computational science, manifesting in materials science as predicting formation energies or elastic moduli from crystal structures. While large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been applied to such tasks, optimal strategies for achieving reliable predictions remain elusive. Here we report fundamental limitations in LLM’s ability to learn from coordinate information in coordinate–category data. Through systematic experiments using synthetic datasets with tunable coordinate and category contributions, and a comprehensive benchmarking framework (MatText), we find that LLMs consistently fail to capture coordinate information while excelling at category patterns. This geometric blindness persists regardless of model size (up to 70 billion parameters), dataset scale (up to 2 × 10 6 structures) or text representation strategy. For material property prediction tasks dominated by structural effects, specialized geometric architectures consistently outperform LLMs, as evidenced by a clear ‘Graph Neural Network Language Model (GNN-LM) wall’ in performance benchmarks. Our analysis provides concrete guidelines for architecture selection in scientific machine learning.

items.title: Less Close but Same Display Rules: Norms for Emotional Expression in Online and Face-to-Face Interactions
items.abstract: Online meetings are increasingly used for work, social, and healthcare purposes, yet their emotional quality is unclear. We tested whether differences in perceived closeness, privacy and anonymity between online and face to face (F2F) interactions alter display rules—the norms governing emotional expression. Participants from Australia (N = 1339) and the United Kingdom (N = 1298) reported display rules for online and F2F interactions with a friend, co-worker, supervisor, GP, or psychologist/counsellor. Online interactions felt less close and comfortable and more anonymous, but display rules did not differ from F2F interactions, with Bayesian analyses strongly supporting the null. Closeness and anonymity predicted display rules only in some cases. Privacy did not, suggesting earlier privacy effects may reflect other factors, such as audience size. Social anxiety was an important predictor, and display rules differed clearly between countries. These findings refine display rule theory and support online platforms for professional and healthcare interactions.
