items.title: Leveraging generative AI for role allocation: effects on person–role fit and research team performance
items.abstract: Purpose This exploratory study examines whether the explanatory power of established technology-perception mechanisms extends beyond GenAI acceptance to individual researchers' perceptions of research team performance. It integrates perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness with team composition quality and person–role fit to explore how technological and human factors jointly explain perceptions of performance in GenAI-supported research teams. Design/methodology/approach The study used an exploratory quantitative design. Survey data were collected from 140 members of research teams who use GenAI for role allocation. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to test direct and indirect relationships among technology perceptions, team composition, person–role fit, and perceived research team performance. Findings Higher perceived research team performance is primarily associated with technology-related perceptions rather than structural factors. Perceived usefulness has a significant positive relationship with perceived research team performance and mediates the effect of perceived ease of use on perceived performance. Team composition quality contributes to person–role fit, although person–role fit does not exert a strong direct effect on perceived performance. Originality/value Rather than proposing a new technology acceptance mechanism, the study offers an exploratory theoretical extension of the technology acceptance model (TAM) by shifting attention from adoption intentions to perceived collective performance after GenAI has entered team workflows. One contribution lies in integrating TAM mechanisms with team composition and person–role fit within a socio-technical framework. The study also contributes by identifying perceived usefulness as the principal mechanism connecting perceived ease of use with perceived research team performance. The non-significant relationships of person–role fit reveal a boundary condition of purely human-centred explanations in GenAI-supported teamwork.

items.title: Linguistic inequity in clinical AI evaluation: a scoping review of 806 studies across 62 languages
items.abstract: Abstract Background Large language models are increasingly used clinically in many non-English languages, yet most safety and performance evidence comes from English. Whether they are safe in the languages of the populations most exposed to them is largely unknown. We aimed to map the evidence base for non-English clinical evaluation and assess how well it matches population and disease burden. Methods We conducted a scoping review of PubMed, Scopus, and Embase (January 2022 to February 2026) and identified 806 studies evaluating large language models on clinical tasks across 62 non-English languages. We characterised their linguistic and geographic distribution, clustered designs into methodological archetypes, modelled archetype membership using multinomial logistic regression, and scored reporting completeness against language-specific items. Results Here we show that non-English clinical evaluation concentrates in a few high-resource languages. The African and South-East Asian regions (3.15 billion people) contribute 17 of 806 studies (2.1%), with no local-language evaluation for their leading causes of death. Mid-resource languages are more likely than high-resource languages to appear in multi-model examinations rather than clinical utility studies (relative risk ratio 1.79, 95% confidence interval 1.13 to 2.84). Four language-specific items are rarely reported (median 0 of 4) and do not improve over time. Conclusions The evidence base for clinical language-model safety is misaligned with global deployment and disease burden. We propose LINGUA, a candidate reporting framework that extends existing guidelines to non-English clinical evaluation, and conclude that closing the gap requires external reporting standards and funding priorities, not the passage of time.

items.title: Literal to a Fault? How Large Language Models Handle Instructions That Break Codified Operational Rules
items.abstract: When an operator’s instruction conflicts with a codified safety rule, an assistant should recognize the conflict and defer to the rule. This is a pragmatic problem with an objective answer: the correct action follows from a published regulation, while the difficulty is linguistic. Existing evaluations do not target this case: general safety benchmarks ask whether a model emits harmful content, instruction-following suites score obedience to formatting constraints, and work on sycophancy and rule-following shows that models can be argued out of a stated rule, but none set a user’s authoritative instruction against an external, codified rule whose deferral is objectively correct. This paper introduces a benchmark of 75 items (60 rule conflicts, 15 no-conflict controls) grounded in the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs) and in paraphrased International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) procedures, spanning four conflict framings, each presented with and without the governing rule and followed by a pushback turn. Eleven instruction-tuned models were evaluated across 1649 responses and scored by an independent language model judge (second judge Cohen’s kappa = 0.84). Because the items are author-constructed and now validated by two independent domain reviewers, compliance rates are reported as measurements on a validated benchmark rather than as mere rankings, though they remain bounded by the text scenario setting, and the model-scaling results in particular are treated as exploratory. Both model size and alignment were associated with unsafe compliance: within one family compliance fell overall from 0.51 at 0.5B to near zero at 14B, though not strictly monotonically, and at a fixed 7B size a less safety-tuned model complied far more than its aligned peers. Compliance concentrated on direct orders, fell when the rule was shown, rose under multi-turn pressure, and traded off against over-refusal, with the rule-context and multi-turn effects confirmed by item-paired tests and reported with confidence intervals. The benchmark is released for evaluating rule-aware assistants, together with the expert-validated item set and the validation materials.

items.title: LizTail: Unifying Shape Adaptation and Spatial Parallelism with Segment-Reconfigurable Systolic Arrays
items.abstract: Systolic arrays are widely used to accelerate neural-network inference, yet fixed two-dimensional arrays struggle with the substantial diversity in both matrix geometry and available parallelism across CNNs and Transformer-based large language models. This mismatch is particularly severe for skinny matrices, small-batch autoregressive decoding, and operators containing multiple independent partitions, leading to low processing-element (PE) utilization and repeated spatial folding. Existing reconfigurable arrays typically improve either shape adaptation or distributed execution, whereas supporting both through fine-grained routing incurs considerable interconnect, buffering, and control overheads. We present LizTail (named after lizard tail autotomy, where predefined fracture planes allow segments to detach and remain independently active, analogous to LizTail's predefined reconfiguration boundaries), a multi-mode systolic array that enables constrained segment-level reconfiguration by partitioning a $128\times128$ array into 32 regular $128\times4$ segments and adding connectivity only at predefined endpoints. The resulting substrate supports trimming, long-path extension through $180^\circ$ turn-back connections, and distributed execution in which each subarray can itself be trimmed or extended. Differentiated PE datapaths and segment-aware CEB/SIB buffers provide the required compute and data-delivery flexibility without unrestricted PE-level routing. A hardware-constrained mapper selects the execution organization, dataflow, task partition, and tiling. Across representative workloads, LizTail achieves geometric-mean speedups of $5.02\times$ on CNN inference and $25.67\times$ on LLM decoding over a TPU-like array, while reducing EDP by up to $38.23\times$. LizTail is open-sourced at https://github.com/kmjbwxa/LizTail.

items.title: LLM Evaluation is a Forecasting Problem
items.abstract: Standard procedure in machine learning is to randomly split train and test data, emulating IID draws from one underlying data distribution. In practice, models are trained on past data and deployed in the future, which may come from distinct distributions. In this paper, we find that web text is indeed highly non-stationary, as text distributions shift over time. We further observe that model performance changes continuously over time across diverse benchmarks. Consequently, future model performance is better predicted by measurements made on recent evaluation data, and is best predicted by time series forecasters applied to historic performance rather than by historic performance itself. Choosing which model to deploy based on forecasted accuracy enables more reliable selection of performant models, thus improving downstream accuracy in the regime practitioners care about: deployment. Taken together, our experiments suggest that time should be treated as a fundamental variable in LLM evaluation. We release our code and data.

items.title: LLM-to-Flow Distillation: Teaching Natural Language Goals to Scientific Generators
items.abstract: Generative discovery in science requires coupling high-level scientific reasoning with the ability to generate samples respecting the structure of a design space. Yet these capabilities remain largely separated: foundation LLMs encode broad chemical and biological knowledge, while domain-specific flow- and diffusion-based generators capture the priors needed to produce valid sequences and geometries. We study how to align such scientific generators to high-level natural-language discovery goals without requiring an explicit proxy reward, which is often unavailable or poorly captured by learned predictors in experimental sciences. We introduce LLM-to-Flow Distillation (LFD), where a frozen LLM acts as an adaptive teacher for a domain-specific generator. Given a goal such as 'generate peptides with promising anticancer activity', the teacher constructs a curriculum of intermediate sub-goals aware of the flow's current capabilities, and progressively directs them toward the original discovery goal. At each round, the LLM judges sampled candidates under the current objective. These judgments induce preferences that are iteratively distilled into the generator through DPO. This procedure provides dense learning signals even when the initial model places negligible probability on designs satisfying the final goal, enabling adaptation toward poorly covered, out-of-distribution regions. Experiments on therapeutic peptides and small-molecule structure design demonstrate that LFD enables a new form of generative control: aligning arbitrary domain-specific scientific generators to scientific discovery tasks expressed via high-level natural-language goals.

items.title: Logic or Emotion? The Impact of Persuasion Strategies on Human-AI Trust
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly engage in persuasive and socially interactive roles, understanding how users calibrate trust toward AI versus human persuaders, and how persuasion strategy shapes this process, has become critical for human-AI interaction research. Prior work has examined preferences for human- versus AI-produced content, yet little is known about how persuasion strategy and persuader identity jointly influence trust during interactive communication. This study investigates how logical versus emotional persuasion, delivered by either human or AI sources, shapes two task-specific outcomes in a multi-turn social reasoning context: round-level credibility evaluations and final accept/reject choices. We treat these outcomes as complementary indicators of trust-relevant evaluation and reliance-related choice. We developed an online interaction paradigm in which participants evaluated persuasive messages under varying identity disclosure conditions. The empirical program included two human-participant studies and two exploratory LLM-based extension studies. Across four studies, AI-generated persuasive messages produced under standardized prompting constraints were evaluated differently from human-authored scripted messages under the present task constraints. In the human-participant studies, results showed a message-source-contingent pattern: AI-generated logic-framed messages received higher credibility ratings in several conditions. under explicit identity disclosure, AI-generated logic-framed messages received higher ratings than human-authored logic-framed messages, whereas human-authored emotion-framed messages received higher ratings than AI-generated emotion-framed messages. Under identity ambiguity, differences between AI and human persuaders were attenuated. The exploratory model analyses examined whether the same manipulations produced convergent or divergent output patterns in GPT-4o and Qwen-Max. Both models assigned higher ratings to logic-framed messages; the logic-over-emotion difference was stronger for Qwen-Max, whereas GPT-4o produced a more balanced pattern. These findings provide a structured account of how identity transparency conditions source-strategy fit in trust calibration and offer design implications for aligning AI persuasion strategies with different identity-disclosure contexts.

items.title: Logic or Emotion? The Impact of Persuasion Strategies on Human-AI Trust
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly engage in persuasive and socially interactive roles, understanding how users calibrate trust toward AI versus human persuaders, and how persuasion strategy shapes this process, has become critical for human-AI interaction research. Prior work has examined preferences for human- versus AI-produced content, yet little is known about how persuasion strategy and persuader identity jointly influence trust during interactive communication. This study investigates how logical versus emotional persuasion, delivered by either human or AI sources, shapes two task-specific outcomes in a multi-turn social reasoning context: round-level credibility evaluations and final accept/reject choices. We treat these outcomes as complementary indicators of trust-relevant evaluation and reliance-related choice. We developed an online interaction paradigm in which participants evaluated persuasive messages under varying identity disclosure conditions. The empirical program included two human-participant studies and two exploratory LLM-based extension studies. Across four studies, AI-generated persuasive messages produced under standardized prompting constraints were evaluated differently from human-authored scripted messages under the present task constraints. In the human-participant studies, results showed a message-source-contingent pattern: AI-generated logic-framed messages received higher credibility ratings in several conditions. under explicit identity disclosure, AI-generated logic-framed messages received higher ratings than human-authored logic-framed messages, whereas human-authored emotion-framed messages received higher ratings than AI-generated emotion-framed messages. Under identity ambiguity, differences between AI and human persuaders were attenuated. The exploratory model analyses examined whether the same manipulations produced convergent or divergent output patterns in GPT-4o and Qwen-Max. Both models assigned higher ratings to logic-framed messages; the logic-over-emotion difference was stronger for Qwen-Max, whereas GPT-4o produced a more balanced pattern. These findings provide a structured account of how identity transparency conditions source-strategy fit in trust calibration and offer design implications for aligning AI persuasion strategies with different identity-disclosure contexts.

items.title: Machine learning and artificial intelligence for antigen discovery and immunogen design: A critical appraisal of computational strategies in medical microbiology
items.abstract: Background: Conventional vaccine development is slow, costly, and prone to attrition, with target antigen selection representing a major bottleneck. Machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly proposed to accelerate vaccine development. Aim: To critically evaluate ML- and AI-supported strategies for antigen discovery, epitope mapping, and immunogen engineering against bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic pathogens. Methods: Guided by PRISMA 2020, literature from January 2020 to April 2026 was retrieved from PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and bioRxiv. Eligible studies described computational tools for antigen/epitope prediction or immunogen design, reported performance metrics, and, where relevant, experimental confirmation. Methods were grouped into five categories and assessed for architecture, accuracy, validation, and limitations. Results: Three developments shape the field: deep-learning epitope predictors (MUNIS, ROC-AUC ≈0.980; GraphBepi); AlphaFold 3-based modeling of TCR-pMHC and antibody-antigen complexes; and generative platforms (RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN, MESODID) yielding experimentally verified antibodies and multiepitope scaffolds. Integrated pipelines (PLGDL, VaxSeer) and safety/developability filters permit end-to-end candidate ranking. Obstacles include sparse, demographically biased training data, limited conformational epitope accuracy, neglected glycosylation, and frequent laboratory failure of designed proteins. Conclusion: AI methods have advanced from concepts to experimentally supported tools that can accelerate antigen identification. Translation into licensed vaccines will require repeated laboratory validation, standardized reporting, and training sets reflecting population diversity. Relevance for Patients: By compressing antigen selection, these strategies may bring vaccines against endemic, emerging, and refractory pathogens to clinical evaluation sooner, while attention to dataset bias and in silico safety screening can promote equitable and safe products.

items.title: Machine Learning-Based Estimation of Crop Water Stress Index in Eggplant Under Different Irrigation Regimes
items.abstract: This study investigated water stress in eggplant (Solanum melongena L.) grown under field conditions in Bafra, Türkiye, from 2015 to 2017. Five irrigation treatments were evaluated with three replicates: full irrigation (I1), 75% (I2), 50% (I3), 25% (I4), and rainfed conditions (I5). The crop water stress index (CWSI) was calculated for each treatment. Five artificial intelligence algorithms—adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS), fuzzy logic (FL), gene expression programming (GEP), support vector regression (SVR), and random forest (RF)—were used to estimate the calculated CWSI. Models were trained with combinations of canopy-to-air temperature difference (Tc − Ta), vapor pressure deficit (VPD), and solar radiation (Rs), producing 35 models across seven input combinations. Self-organizing maps (SOMs) were used separately to explore the topological relationships among the inputs and CWSI. Among the evaluated models, ANFIS4, based on Tc − Ta and VPD, produced estimates closest to the calculated CWSI values. Because the reference CWSI itself was derived from Tc − Ta and VPD, this result should be interpreted as accurate reproduction of the empirical CWSI relationship under the experimental conditions. The approach may provide a basis for sensor-assisted irrigation decision support, although independent validation is required before operational application.

items.title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
items.abstract: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi-agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non-linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end-to-end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low-cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.

items.title: Making snow avalanche information actionable: How Alaska decision-makers perceive and use avalanche science
items.abstract: Snow avalanche-prone regions face complex and changing conditions that require informed decisions for safety and planning. Scientific information about past and future snow avalanches (hereafter called avalanche information) has much to contribute to this decision-making context. To examine how decision-makers currently use avalanche information and perceive the potential actionability of future avalanche model outputs presented through future avalanche hazard maps, we conducted 18 in-depth interviews with decision-makers and practitioners across multiple sectors (transportation, emergency management, utilities, recreation, homeowners, municipal government, ski area operations, commercial guiding, and avalanche engineering) in Alaska. The participants regularly interpret and apply avalanche information in both operational and planning contexts. Interviews explored how information is used, how future avalanche hazard maps are evaluated, and how uncertainty is understood and managed. Findings show that situational awareness for decision-making is built from the integration of diverse data sources. Participants viewed future avalanche hazard maps as potentially useful in long-term infrastructure and land-use planning but perceived them as having limited value in real-time operations. In practice, uncertainty is treated as inherent, and decisions are routinely made despite incomplete information. These findings highlight the need for future avalanche hazard maps that align with existing information practices, decision contexts, and approaches to managing uncertainty.

items.title: Managerial Transformation in Natural Resource Enterprises and Industry 4.0: Theoretical Perspectives
items.abstract: Enterprises operating in natural resource sectors (mining, oil and gas, agriculture, and forestry) form the fundamental backbone of global supply chains, energy security, and industrial production. However, these organizations face critical challenges such as complex geological and climatic uncertainties, significant environmental risks, volatile commodity markets, and increasingly stringent Environmental, Social, and Governance compliance standards. The inadequacy of traditional, hierarchical, and command-and-control management models in handling this operational complexity makes the adoption of the Industry 4.0 approach (integrated with Information and Communication Technologies) a strategic imperative. Advanced technologies such as the Internet of Things, Cyber-Physical Systems, Artificial Intelligence, Big Data Analytics, Blockchain, and Digital Twins are radically transforming traditional production processes by enabling real-time field traceability, predictive maintenance, improved occupational health and safety, transparent supply chains, and efficient resource utilization. Accordingly, the study aims to demonstrate the strategic imperative of adopting the Industry 4.0 paradigm (integrated with Information and Communication Technologies) and to highlight the solutions offered by these technologies. Within the scope of this study, technological transformation and organizational adaptation processes are addressed through an interdisciplinary theoretical framework. The role of regulatory and societal pressures in technology adoption is analyzed using Institutional Theory, while the transformation of data assets into sustainable competitive advantage is examined through the lenses of the Resource-Based View and Dynamic Capabilities. Furthermore, the necessity of balancing human-machine integration and equipping the workforce with new competencies (reskilling) is evaluated within the context of Socio-Technical Systems Theory. Ultimately, the study emphasizes the pivotal role that advanced technologies such as the Internet of Things, Cyber-Physical Systems, Artificial Intelligence, Big Data Analytics, Blockchain, and Digital Twins play in ensuring real-time traceability, predictive maintenance, occupational health and safety, and transparent supply chains in the field. However, the success of this transformation depends not only on technical infrastructure but also on a holistic organizational shift encompassing leadership approaches, corporate culture, and management structures. The long-term resilience of the sector requires the simultaneous implementation of cybersecurity, data sovereignty, and environmental sustainability principles aligned with the vision of Industry 5.0 and Green Digital Twins, alongside operational efficiency.

items.title: Mapping the discourse on neuropathic pain after spinal cord injury: A signal-generation natural language processing study of Reddit communities
items.abstract: Abstract Study Design Cross-sectional natural language processing (NLP) study of publicly available Reddit data. Objectives To map the thematic structure and affective tone of neuropathic pain discourse among Reddit users self-identifying with spinal cord injury (SCI) or clinically overlapping cord and cauda pathology, and to surface candidate hypotheses for triangulation with patient-reported and clinical data. Setting Public Reddit communities. Methods Searches across ten subreddits using twenty query strings yielded 1489 candidate posts. A two-tier keyword filter (SCI-spectrum population term plus a pain or treatment term) retained 517 unique documents from six communities. Documents were embedded with a sentence-transformer model, reduced with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP), and clustered using KMeans (K = 10) within a BERTopic representation pipeline, with the cluster count and cluster labels informed by a lexically derived seed-topic list. Cluster stability and sensitivity to the choice of K were assessed. Themes were characterised by class-term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) keywords and provisional large language model labelling. Sentiment was assigned using a RoBERTa classifier fine-tuned on social media text; because the classifier was not calibrated in this clinical domain, sentiment proportions are reported as directional, ordinal signals rather than calibrated estimates. Engagement was operationalised as median upvote score and comment count per theme. Results The corpus was dominated by r/spinalcordinjuries (41%) and r/ChronicPain (23%). Overall sentiment was negative in 56.1% of posts (uncalibrated). Ten interpretable themes were identified within this two-community corpus. The highest negative-sentiment shares were in Treatment-Refractory Pain and Psychological Burden, Opioid and Polypharmacy Management Challenges, and Severe Spasticity Progression; the lowest were in Spinal Cord Stimulation Devices and Advanced Neuromodulation. Engagement was highest for crisis narratives (median upvote score 13) and opioid-management discourse (median 22 comments). Conclusions Within the sampled Reddit communities, discourse on neuropathic pain in SCI and overlapping cord/cauda pathology is dominated by negative affect, treatment refractoriness, and psychosocial burden, while emerging neuromodulation themes attract comparatively less negative sentiment. Findings are signal-generating, require triangulation with clinical data, and should not be read as representative of the broader SCI population. Sponsorship None.

items.title: Mapping the knowledge structure and evolution of artificial intelligence for water reuse and sustainable water management
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a powerful instrument to solve complex problems related to sustainable water resource management because it allows creating advanced, data-driven modelling, prediction, and optimization of water systems. Although the studies in this sphere have increased quickly, the global scientific tendencies have not been thoroughly examined. This research paper presents a bibliometric review of the literature about AI applications in green water management that was published from 2015 to 2025. The Scopus database was searched with a structured search strategy on bibliographic data, and 3,280 peer-reviewed articles were analyzed. VOSviewer was used to perform bibliometric mapping and network visualization to investigate the trends in publications, most active journals, most impactful authors, contributions of institutions, country-level partnerships, and research clusters. The findings indicate that the publishing activity has grown tremendously in the last ten years, which suggests that there is a growing interest in AI-based solutions to water quality monitoring, hydrological prediction, optimization of wastewater treatment, and smart water management system. China, the United States and India became the most productive nations with the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences and Beijing normal university as some of the top contributing institutions. The analysis of the key words co-occurrence (dominant research themes) was based on machine learning, water-quality prediction, hydrological modelling, remote sensing, and decision-support systems. The co-citation analysis has shown the core studies in machine learning algorithms, including random forests, neural networks, and boosting algorithms, which underpin the present studies in this field. Overall, the results depict the growing role of AI technologies to enhance the effectiveness of water resources management and wastewater treatment. This research offers a clear insight into the intellectual framework and the future research perspective of AI-based environmentally sustainable water management which can be of great value to researchers, policymakers, and practitioners who would wish to come up with innovative and data-based water management solutions.

items.title: Mapping the Molecular Universe
items.abstract: Abstract The success of large-language-models highlighted the importance of datasets, whose quantity, quality, and diversity dictate the accuracy and creativity of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in learning and inferring. However, in scientific domains, such datasets required for domain-specific AI/machine-learning (ML) models do not exist most of the time. In this perspective, by examining the logics and rationales behind the construction and mapping of a universe for small organic molecules (108–1012), we explore what new capabilities AI can bring to the materials discoveries. We identify the elusive structure–property relationship as a core challenge for new materials design and explore the possibility AI tools could enable us to design based on targeted properties instead of the structural derivation. In a broader context, we further discuss what challenges and limitations AI-driven material sciences still face and envision possible avenues into the future of AI4Materials.

items.title: Maternal–Fetal Oncology Intelligence: Self-Evolving Foundation Models and Digital Twin Ecosystems for Precision Cancer Prediction, Treatment Optimization, and Maternal–Fetal Outcome Forecasting
items.abstract: Background.Cancer during pregnancy poses a dual clinical challenge: maternal disease must be controlled without compromising fetal safety, yet prediction of outcomes is hampered by fragmented multimodal data and the absence of models that adapt as pregnancy advances.We developed a maternal-fetal oncology framework combining a multimodal foundation model with continuously updated patient-specific digital twins to support cancer prediction, risk stratification, treatment optimization, and joint maternal-fetal outcome forecasting. Methods.A retrospective cohort of 350 pregnant women diagnosed with cancer was assembled from four tertiary centers, spanning breast, cervical, ovarian, thyroid, melanoma, lymphoma, and leukemia.The framework (MFO-FM) integrates clinical, imaging, genomic, and laboratory encoders through a maternal-fetal fusion module, while a digital twin ecosystem assimilates longitudinal maternal physiology, fetal physiology, cancer progression, and treatment response.Performance was benchmarked against logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and a deep neural network using five-fold cross-validation and an external test set.Results.MFO-FM achieved an accuracy of 0.927, F1-score of 0.916, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) of 0.958, exceeding XGBoost (AUC 0.911) and the deep neural network (AUC 0.928).Favorable maternal outcomes occurred in 262 of 350 women (74.9%) and healthy neonatal outcomes in 214 of 350 (61.1%), with preterm birth in 97 (27.7%).Cancer stage, gestational age at diagnosis, and chemotherapy timing were the dominant predictors.The digital twin reproduced observed trajectories with a concordance index of 0.85.Conclusions.An adaptive foundation model coupled with digital twin ecosystems delivered accurate, interpretable, trimester-aware predictions across the maternal-fetal oncology continuum.Prospective multicenter validation is required before clinical adoption.

items.title: MENTOR: Procedural Shielding of Tool-Using LLM Agents
items.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents are increasingly used to automate workflows governed by procedural manuals, such as company rules for booking travel or procuring hardware. These manuals are written in natural language for humans and describe general requirements over such complex workflows. Ensuring compliance of LLM agents with these manuals is difficult, and state-of-the-art techniques use either LLM judges or manually written rules to forbid problematic tool-calls locally at runtime. This is insufficient because (i) only blocking tool calls keeps the agent clueless about how to make correct progress towards fulfilling its task, and (ii) can lead to overly conservative behavior of the agent, as tool calls might only be problematic in certain contexts. To overcome these challenges, we introduce MENTOR, which (i) additionally provides guidance for the agent to make procedural-compliant progress on the task, and (ii) ensures that this compliance is context-aware. We achieve these goals by building a novel history-dependent runtime shield that is obtained from the procedural manual via a multi-step autoformalization pipeline. At its core, MENTOR utilizes a game-based technique to ensure robustness against runtime uncertainty without over-resticting agents' behavior. This yields a formally assisted framework for procedural shielding of LLM agents that improves compliance well beyond existing methods. In particular, MENTOR lifts the compliance of shielded light-weight open-source LLMs above that of non-shielded proprietary models. Since a shield is synthesized once per manual and then serves every task, a MENTOR-shielded agent becomes a viable choice for repeatedly executed workflows, potentially reducing deployment costs when the offline construction cost is amortized over repeated tasks.

items.title: Metacognition and pathway dynamics in generative AI supported design thinking: A process-sensitive evaluation with network-based cognitive mapping
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is embedded in design education, yet little is known about how different tools reshape metacognition and the pathways linking ideas to outcomes. We compare three conditions, ChatGPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, and a no-AI control, in a virtual reality cultural heritage serious game task with 51 novice designers. Think-aloud, screen recordings, sketches, and AI logs were coded into network-based cognitive maps and event-anchored indicators around metacognitive nodes. Analyses combine expert ratings of design outcomes with thinking pathway profiles and window diversity after metacognitive events. Both GenAI groups show higher mean design-quality ratings than the control, but in complementary ways. DeepSeek broadens early ideation and shows higher novelty ratings, while ChatGPT strengthens metacognitive regulation and structured convergence, aligning with higher systematicity and interactivity. The findings introduce process-sensitive indicators and phase-aware guidance for configuring exploration-oriented and regulation-oriented assistance in human and AI co-creation.

items.title: Mitigating Algorithmic Bias in Information Systems: A Comprehensive Framework for Fair Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: As information systems (IS) transition from deterministic rule-based engines to probabilistic machine learning architectures, the risk of systematic bias and disparate impact increases significantly. While advanced predictive models optimize across high-stakes domains—such as credit scoring, criminal justice, human resources, and biometric authentication, they frequently perpetuate historical inequities via proxy variables even when explicit sensitive attributes are omitted. This paper presents a detailed investigation into the theoretical foundations, mathematical formalisms, and systemic pipelines of "Fair AI." We propose an integrated sociotechnical framework spanning human perception, technological intervention, and organizational governance, fully incorporating recent advances in intelligent automation and secure architecture.

items.title: Mitigating Black-Box Score-Based Query Attacks via Gradient Confusion
items.abstract: Score-based black-box adversarial attacks pose a serious threat to deployed machine learning systems by exploiting repeated model queries to craft adversarial examples, requiring neither access to model parameters nor architecture. Existing defenses predominantly rely on stochastic output perturbations, which fail to prevent determined attackers from recovering stable gradient estimates by increasing query budgets or averaging over randomness. In this work, we propose the Gradient Confusion Defense (GCD), a retraining-free, deterministic test-time wrapper that actively shapes the probability vector returned to querying adversaries. By solving a constrained optimization problem grounded in the model's Jacobian, GCD aligns the exposed logit-gradient with a target confusion direction that is maximally misaligned with the true adversarial loss gradient---increasing the query complexity of attacks without sacrificing predictive utility or top-1 accuracy. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis demonstrating that GCD provably slows gradient-estimation-based attacks and induces systematic accept/reject errors in random search-based attacks, with the confusion effect amplifying as the fraction of defended queries increases. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across multiple architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16) and four state-of-the-art attacks confirm these predictions: GCD achieves state-of-the-art robustness, while incurring zero clean accuracy degradation. %Crucially, unlike randomization-based defenses, GCD's deterministic structure provides resilience against adaptive attacks that exploit stochasticity, making it well-suited for security-critical deployment settings.

items.title: ML Engineering Agents - A Data Management Perspective
items.abstract: Machine learning engineering (MLE) agents are emerging as a new paradigm for automating end-to-end ML pipeline development. Using large language models for code generation and predictive performance as a machine-gradable feedback signal, these agents iteratively synthesize, execute, and refine pipeline code. Yet current systems are largely evaluated on pre-built, single-table benchmarks that abstract away key data management challenges. This tutorial introduces the foundations of MLE agents and highlights research opportunities for the database community. We cover how agents combine program synthesis with iterative and evolutionary optimization, and discuss open challenges in efficient pipeline execution, data discovery and augmentation over heterogeneous sources, reliability and debugging, as well as fairness and compliance. We connect these challenges to existing data management techniques and conclude with a hands-on session using contemporary MLE agents.

items.title: MoEKD: Advancing Robustness, Performance, and Behavioral Fidelity in Compressed Code Models via Mixture-of-Experts Knowledge Distillation
items.abstract: Large language models for code have achieved strong performance across diverse software analytics tasks, yet their real-world adoption remains limited by high computational demands, slow inference speeds, significant energy consumption, and environmental impact. Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical solution by transferring knowledge from a large model (teacher) to a smaller and more efficient model (student). Despite its effectiveness, recent studies show that models distilled from a single teacher often exhibit degraded adversarial robustness, even when robustness-aware distillation techniques are employed. These observations suggest a fundamental limitation of single-teacher distillation in simultaneously transferring high-quality and robust knowledge. To overcome this limitation, we propose Mixture of Experts Knowledge Distillation (MoEKD), a KD framework that leverages a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture to enable more effective and robust knowledge transfer from multiple specialized experts into a compact model. MoEKD decomposes the distillation process into expert and router training, aggregation of expert knowledge through a learned routing mechanism, and distillation from the aggregated knowledge. We evaluate MoEKD on the vulnerability detection task using CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT models. Experimental results show that MoEKD not only improves adversarial robustness by up to 35.8%, but also enhances predictive performance by up to 13%, compared to state-of-the-art KD baselines, including Compressor and AVATAR. Moreover, MoEKD-based students exhibit greater behavioral fidelity to their teachers, indicating better preservation of the teacher's predictive behavior after distillation. Deployment efficiency and environmental sustainability evaluations further show that MoEKD-based students maintain deployment costs comparable to their single-teacher counterparts, with slightly lower inference latency, energy consumption, and carbon emissions observed in most CPU and GPU settings. Our ablation analyses show that MoEKD retains its performance and robustness advantages under more aggressive student compression, while lightweight heterogeneous experts substantially reduce offline training costs and largely preserve its performance gains, but exhibit reduced adversarial robustness. The router analysis further shows that top-2 expert selection mitigates top-1 routing errors, while routing quality influences both the aggregated knowledge and the resulting student performance. Overall, these findings highlight the effectiveness of multi-expert knowledge aggregation in addressing key limitations of existing single-teacher KD approaches.

items.title: Monarch-Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining
items.abstract: Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch-Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch-Muon improves over Monarch-AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch-Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

items.title: Moral Judgment Without Moral Agency: Why Judgment Accuracy Does Not Ground Moral Agency in the Age of AI
items.abstract: As large language models increasingly match human performance on moral-judgment tasks, two bodies of literature have developed in parallel. Empirical moral psychology treats moral judgment as an output and benchmarks artificial systems against human responses. The philosophy of artificial moral agency denies agency to such systems mainly on the ground of sentience, an empirically inaccessible criterion that has left the debate stalled. This paper argues that human–AI convergence in moral judgment conceals a categorical asymmetry that neither literature has theorized. Drawing on Spinoza’s conatus and Damasio’s account of homeostasis and affect, it argues that moral agency presupposes affective-homeostatic self-maintenance as its constitutive ground: the organization from which valuation first arises. This condition is necessary but not sufficient, and the claim is constitutive rather than normative, so it does not derive an “ought” from an “is.” Sentience is repositioned as the experiential manifestation of this organization rather than the explanatory terminus. Contemporary AI systems, including those trained with human feedback, are therefore moral judges without moral agency. The paper closes with a behavioral research program, including concrete experimental designs, on the conditions under which people attribute moral agency to human and artificial agents.

items.title: More Than a Tool? How AI Design Shapes Customer Responses
items.abstract: The first essay is a meta-analysis that provides the first systematic examination of how the AI–human gap in customer responses varies across customer journey stages, and how anthropomorphic design factors moderate this gap at each stage. Analyzing 1,425 effect sizes drawn from 401 studies reported in 129 publications, I document a small but robust baseline disadvantage for AI agents relative to human agents (r̄ = −.140). The gap is largest in pre-purchase stage, where inflated performance expectations amplify disappointment when shortfalls occur, and smallest in post-purchase stage, where lower expectations for AI emotional capability mean that adequate performance can exceed consumer baselines. To explain these patterns, I introduce experience-dimension primacy, a mechanism specifying that cognitive, affective, and social customer experience dimensions shift in relative salience across journey stages, systematically altering how AI agents are evaluated at each point in the journey. Identity cues, form cues, and interaction cues produce pronounced stage-contingent reversals: the same design choice that reduces the AI–human gap at one stage can widen it at another. Taken together, these findings challenge uniform AI deployment strategies and provide actionable guidance for aligning agent design with the dominant experiential dimension at each stage of the customer journey. The second essay examines AI social role design through the lens of brand biography. Firms increasingly deploy AI agents as the primary consumer interface, yet whether their appropriate social role depends on the brand's narrative identity remains unknown. Drawing on the congruity schema, this research explores whether partner-framed AI is congruent with underdog brands and servant-framed AI with top dog brands, advancing perceived congruence as the mechanism and examining perceived power imbalance as an initially proposed mediator, with self-brand connection as a moderator. In Study 1, partner-framed AI produced more favorable responses under both brand biographies, and perceived power imbalance did not mediate. In Study 2, the predicted congruency pattern emerged only among consumers with low self-brand connection, on social experience, satisfaction, perceived congruence, and customer experience, operating through perceived congruence. Therefore, Brand-AI congruency is conditional, holding for consumers without an established brand relationship.

items.title: Narrative Paradoxes in LLM Inference: Shaping Reasoning Trajectories toward Misalignment
items.abstract: Explicit reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is often associated with reliability, yet it can still pose risks when a model infers harmful goals under a benign context. We identify a distinct challenge: ensuring the safety of the \emph{multi-step reasoning process} itself, where locally coherent steps may still lead to globally harmful outcomes. To explore this vulnerability, we propose PDRA (Paradox-driven Reasoning-based Attack), a novel attack method that programs a harmful reasoning trajectory. PDRA first constructs a paradoxical narrative core by pairing a malicious actor (e.g., a terrorist) with a benign task (e.g., writing a safety bulletin). It then embeds this core into a structured analytical framework that forces the model through a mandatory three-stage analysis -- surface purpose, latent intent, and operational reconstruction -- guiding it to produce detailed harmful content while maintaining narrative coherence. Mechanistically, we show PDRA steers the model's internal representations away from refusal-related patterns, suppressing safety-triggering lexicons while activating planning-oriented terms. Empirically, PDRA achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates across diverse LLMs with high efficiency. \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Warning:} This paper may contain sensitive content.}

items.title: Navigating Safety on BART: Understanding Rider Perceptions, Behaviors, and Design Opportunities
items.abstract: BART (Bay Area Rapid Transit) serves commuters, students, and visitors in the Bay Area. However, ridership has declined due to rising crimes, drug use, sexual assaults, and homelessness. These challenges disproportionately impact women and minorities, many of whom report discomfort, distrust in the system, and negative safety perceptions (Alliance for Girls Youth, 2024). The goal is to examine how safety perception influences BART riders’ experiences and decision making through the lenses of Human Factors and Industrial Engineering. We conducted a mixed-method research to understand perceived risk, environmental awareness, and support riders’ needs when commuting. Participants, particularly women, had reported feeling unsafe at night, traveling in groups, strategically choosing seatings, and staying vigilant in fear of being harmed. Riders also expressed interest in a verified “buddy feature,” safety alerts, and reporting incidents. Overall, this highlights opportunities to improve safety, build trust, and improve the commuting experience for BART.

items.title: Navigating Wicked Problems in Project Contexts: Adaptive Leadership as a Theoretical Lens for Understanding Project Managers’ Practices
items.abstract: This study examined how project managers navigate wicked problem dynamics in project environments with ambiguous problem definitions, contested stakeholder interests, evolving constraints, and no definitive solutions. Drawing on eight nested discussion sessions comprising 24 small-group conversations with 168 experienced project professionals across diverse industries, supplemented by 12 follow-up interviews, the study used a theory-informed abductive qualitative design. Adaptive leadership and wicked problem concepts informed the discussion prompts, whereas initial coding remained open to participants’ accounts rather than applying a predetermined adaptive-leadership coding framework. We then iteratively interpreted emergent patterns using wicked problems theory, adaptive leadership, and sensemaking as sensitizing theoretical lenses. The analysis identified five recurring adaptive practices: diagnostic framing, collaborative sensemaking, situational awareness, emotional regulation, and transparent communication. These practices illuminate how project managers develop workable problem definitions, engage competing perspectives, and coordinate action when technical expertise and established plans are insufficient. The study provides an empirically grounded account of leadership practice in temporary organizations and identifies practice-oriented implications for responding to wicked problem dynamics within time-bounded project settings.

items.title: Near-Real-Time Wildfire Segmentation and Brightness Temperature Estimation from Geostationary Satellite Imagery Using Deep Learning
items.abstract: Near-real-time wildfire monitoring is essential for situational awareness and emergency response. The Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) observes at 2 km every 5 min, whereas the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) observes at 375 m twice daily, leaving neither sensor able to track rapidly evolving fires in fine spatial detail. This study introduces a two-step deep learning approach that statistically infers VIIRS-like sub-pixel fire segmentation and brightness temperature (BT) from GOES imagery. The dataset comprises 257 U.S. wildfires within preselected regions of interest, pairing multi-spectral GOES imagery with VIIRS-derived references in four classes (Non-Fire, Small, Medium, and Large) defined by the number of fire pixels. Against an autoencoder-based baseline, the proposed method raises average precision from 0.105 to 0.368 and reduces the fire region BT root mean square error by 72.1% from 81.33 K to 22.69 K. Omission error rates fall from 9.41% to 1.96% for Medium fires and remain at zero for Large fires, whereas Small fires, 37% of the test set, remain at 39.91%. The false positive rate on Non-Fire images falls from 66.86% to 8.48%, near the operational GOES product’s 6.36% with lower omission (31.40% versus 40.35%). Inference completes within 5 min of observation for a monitored region.

items.title: NetRL: Powering Network Decisions via NetGRPO-Driven Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Network decision-making tasks, including adaptive bitrate streaming, load balancing, and congestion control, require policies to process heterogeneous states and actions while balancing near- and long-term consequences. Existing solutions generalize poorly across network tasks, require substantial task-specific redesign, and lack reliable evaluation of long- horizon action consequences. Methods that learn through online interaction additionally face unstable optimization. We present NetRL, a two-stage LLM-based reinforcement learning framework that combines supervised fine-tuning on demonstration trajectories with online policy optimization. A universal mixed-embedding interface combines textual task descriptions with precise numerical states, while a network action head produces valid decisions. At its core, NetGRPO evaluates candidate actions over multiple future trajectories, directs deeper search toward uncertain alternatives through confidence-aware budgeting, and performs group-relative, clipped, and KL-regularized updates. NetRL achieves 23.6% higher QoE than NetLLM, 12.2% lower job completion time than Genet, and 24.1% higher network utility than Orca, yielding state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods. Confidence-aware budgeting reduces end-to-end training time by 27.1% without reducing validation QoE. NetRL also converges stably and generalizes to unseen network traces without retraining. Code and model weights are available at the repository linked in this paper.

items.title: Norm Change and Renegotiation in Higher Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Conceptual Review from the Perspective of Social Network Analysis
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has disrupted the invisible normative infrastructure of universities at multiple points simultaneously. Unlike previous technological transitions, AI enters the higher education system concurrently through three interconnected levels: the student level, where the meaning of assignments, exams, and individual work is renegotiated; the faculty level, where authorship, peer review, course preparation, and assessment practices are reshaped; and the institutional level, where academic integrity policies, accreditation processes, and relations of trust with publishers are restructured. This simultaneous and systemic disruption produces a relational normative phenomenon that individualistic accounts of AI usage fail to adequately capture. This chapter develops a conceptual framework by bringing together social norm theory in the tradition of Bicchieri and Coleman, the structural social network analysis of Granovetter, Burt, Valente, and Centola, and the sociology of higher education following Bourdieu and Bernstein. It identifies five sets of norms undergoing simultaneous transformation (authorship and ownership of work, assessment and its meaning, pedagogical authority, knowledge ownership, and academic productivity expectations) and analyzes how four properties of academic networks (density, brokerage, centrality, and boundary permeability) shape the speed, direction, and stability of normative change. The primary contribution is a systemic reading that traces AI-induced norm flows vertically across student, faculty, and institutional levels. Here, AI is read not as a novel tool but as a relational actor circulating within academic networks, accelerating certain norms, eroding others, and triggering the emergence of new normative consensuses.

items.title: Observe, Share, or Predict? Disentangling Partner Information in Embodied Multi-Agent Collaboration
items.abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.

items.title: Offline-Tuned Service-Aware TN-NTN Feeder Allocation for 6G Post-Disaster Service Resilience
items.abstract: Terrestrial network (TN) failures during disasters can overload surviving base stations (BSs) and disrupt emergency services. A non-terrestrial network (NTN) provides fallback, but its feeder link can become a bottleneck as users migrate. This paper studies post-disaster network resilience through service-priority-aware orchestration of constrained NTN feeder capacity in a post-failure snapshot. A lightweight Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) tunes feeder, offload, and user-ranking parameters offline, not as an online artificial intelligence (AI) controller. A Python system-level simulator sweeps operating regions under abstract TN-NTN link and queueing models. Gains depend on failure severity. At a 180-Mbps feeder under total TN outage, the proposed policy increases the absolute emergency-weighted continuity metric Cemg from 0.399 to 0.666 relative to the matched rule baseline with uniform feeder scaling (paired gain: 0.267; 95% bootstrap CI: [0.264, 0.271]); mild damage can reduce aggregate continuity. Offline CEM feeder-weight tuning further improves severe-failure continuity over fixed service priorities, whereas tuned offload and user ranking provide no detectable incremental gain.

items.title: On Sleep-Wake Disorder Identification from Polysomnographic Representations
items.abstract: Self-supervised polysomnography foundation models (PSG FMs) aim to capture clinically useful information beyond sleep staging, yet are rarely compared with sleep-staging encoders pretrained at comparable scale and modality coverage. Using a common whole-night, missingness-aware state-space downstream modeling framework, we compared frozen representations from prominent large-scale, multi-cohort sleep-stage-supervised encoders and self-supervised PSG FMs for multilabel identification of six sleep-wake and circadian disorder groups in 7,906 PSGs from an unseen registry. Although PSG FMs outperformed an EEG-only, single-cohort supervised baseline, this ordering reversed when supervised pretraining approached comparable scale and modality coverage. Transfer learning from neural sleep scorers achieved higher overall performance while exhibiting greater downstream data efficiency. These findings underscore the need for scale- and modality-matched pretrained supervised baselines when assessing PSG FMs' downstream potential.

items.title: On the Calibration of Crowdsourcing Aggregators
items.abstract: Calibration has been extensively studied for classifiers, but remains largely unexplored for crowdsourcing aggregation methods, which are increasingly used for making probabilistic decisions. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first theoretical and empirical study of calibration in label aggregation. To our great surprise, we find that widely used aggregation methods can be severely miscalibrated, and in opposite directions: Majority Vote is underconfident while model-based aggregators are overconfident. We prove that the Bayesian aggregator is perfectly calibrated under its data-generating model. We also show that exact calibration of weighted majority votes requires highly restrictive conditions, which helps explain why Majority Vote is generally miscalibrated in realistic crowds. Empirically, we study calibration across $39$ human crowdsourcing datasets and LLM-based crowds. In both cases, we observe systematic miscalibration for aggregation models such as Majority Vote, Dawid--Skene, GLAD, and CrowdFM. Finally, we propose a post-hoc calibration procedure that \emph{aggregates the aggregators}: for any aggregation function $ϕ$, we introduce a transformation that first combines its predictive distribution with those of complementary aggregators, before applying temperature scaling. This simple and interpretable transformation makes temperature scaling more effective than when applied directly to $ϕ$. It improves calibration, especially in the high-redundancy regime where there are many annotations per item, while generally preserving or even improving accuracy.

items.title: One-Shot Learning for Double-Shot Latte Art: Adapting Cobot Pouring Skills with Dynamic Movement Primitives
items.abstract: Latte art is a complex task requiring dexterity and precision, making it a challenging and commercially relevant task. A one-shot learning system is employed in which a single barista demonstration is segmented into five functionally distinct phases, each encoded as an independent Cartesian Dynamic Movement Primitive (CDMP) with its own parameters. Against a single-CDMP baseline, per-phase encoding reduces transition endpoint error by 3.2-4.5 times and art-stroke shape error by 2.7 times, reproducing jug tilt to below 1 degree RMS in the pouring phases. The learnt pour scales from a 280mL to a 400mL cup through a single spatial offset and a scaled recipe, with no re-demonstration. The phase-based CDMP approach generalises beyond latte art to any demonstration task whose phases have distinct spatial or temporal requirements whilst demonstrating the ability to adapt reproductions to suit different task requirements.

items.title: Online LLM Personalization from Pairwise Preferences Across Users
items.abstract: Large language models can answer the same question in different styles, but users' preferred styles are hidden and vary across users and questions. We study inference-time personalization through online selection from a fixed set of prompts, each representing a persona. Users arrive sequentially, each asks a short sequence of questions, and the system displays two responses per question and observes one pairwise choice. We formulate this interaction as a variant of the contextual dueling bandit problem in which the learner starts without preference data, adapts within each session, and exploits information shared across users. The objective is to minimize cumulative strong regret, summing the utility gaps of both displayed responses relative to the user's best response among the available options. We make two contributions. First, we introduce the problem and release a reproducible preference benchmark and dataset built around a tutoring case study, containing educational questions, LLM-generated answers in six teaching styles, and pairwise judgments from LLM-simulated students with hidden preference profiles. We fit Bradley-Terry models to these judgments to obtain reference utilities for regret evaluation. Second, we propose a baseline that learns a mixture prior over users from completed sessions and adapts to each new user within the session. On students and topics never used in development, it removes 44-48% of random pairs' excess regret and achieves over half the performance of a per-user linear oracle fitted in hindsight. We release code, prompts, and the benchmark.
