items.title: Opening ecological data to reduce bias and strengthen AI in ecology
items.abstract: In 1985, Richard Stallman introduced copyleft, a licensing principle that allows source code to be used, modified, and redistributed provided that the same freedoms are preserved in derivative works (Stallman, 1985). Although developed for software, copyleft offers a useful analogy for ecological research, where data, metadata, and analytical code should be accessible and reusable under clear licenses. Similarly, our ability to understand and address ecological challenges such as biodiversity loss, species range shifts, land degradation, and climate change depends on ecological knowledge being open where ethically appropriate and otherwise responsibly accessible. Such knowledge should also be managed according to the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) and established domain standards such as Darwin Core and Ecological Metadata Language (Wieczorek et al. 2012, Wilkinson et al. 2016). Despite substantial progress in open science (Dwivedi et al. 2022), many key ecological datasets (e.g., national ecological inventories, biodiversity records, and high-spatial- and temporal-resolution remote-sensing data) remain proprietary or available only with restricted access (e.g., requiring formal approval). These gaps are substantial: Large-scale analyses of hundreds of millions of ecological records reveal persistent taxonomic, geographic, and temporal biases (Meyer et al. 2015, Daru and Rodriguez, 2023). Much of the scientific literature also remains behind paywalls, while open-access publication fees can create barriers for researchers with limited funding (Rocchini and Neteler 2012). This paradox, that is, publicly funded knowledge becoming inaccessible to the public, constrains who can participate in ecological research and which ecosystems, regions, and perspectives are ultimately represented. AI does not create this problem but can amplify it by embedding data biases in models reused at scale, while closed training data limit independent scrutiny (Koch et al. 2022). AI for ecology encompasses task-specific machine-learning and computer-vision models, as well as foundation models, including large language models (LLMs). These systems differ in scale, purpose, and accessibility, but all depend on the quality, documentation, and governance of the data used to train and evaluate them. By integrating diverse data sources, AI can transform ecological research. However, when data, code, or model-development processes cannot be independently inspected, existing knowledge gaps and biases may be transferred into ecological inference. Appropriately open, reliable, and interoperable ecological data, together with transparent and auditable AI infrastructures, are therefore essential for robust, equitable, and epistemically sound ecological research. The expansion of AI in ecological research intensifies the need for transparent and well-documented knowledge. Bias is not unique to AI: statistical, mechanistic, and machine-learning models can all inherit limitations from their data and assumptions. AI can increase the scale, opacity, and reach of these effects (Han et al. 2023). Currently, many applications in ecology use task-specific AI models trained for bounded prediction or classification problems (Pichler and Hartig 2023). These models are often trained on specialized aggregated ecological repositories (e.g., biodiversity data from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility [GBIF]), climatic variables (e.g., from WorldClim and ERA5), or land-use and land cover change mapping (e.g., from satellite imagery). In contrast, the rise of foundation models, including LLMs used for the automated synthesis of scientific literature, code generation, data processing and analysis, requires massive cross-domain training sets that are difficult to build from scratch. Consequently, models trained on skewed, geographically biased, or inaccessible datasets can systematically misrepresent under-sampled regions and reflect long-standing inequities in ecological knowledge. When training datasets are inaccessible, their composition is also difficult to inspect, making gaps in the representation of regions, languages, taxa, or perspectives harder to detect and evaluate. Thus, LLMs are not necessarily more biased than task-specific AI models, but their biases can be harder to trace and hence propagate across a wider range of users, tasks, and applications. In ecology, both task-specific and generic models inherit the limitations of the data used to train them. For example, species-recognition models inherit taxonomic imbalances in training images (Koch et al. 2022), whereas LLMs can process ecological information rapidly but may perform poorly on specific tasks. Gougherty and Clipp (2024) found that LLMs often struggled to extract pathogen-incidence values and sometimes inferred that all individuals were affected when no incidence value was reported. Similarly, Dorm et al. (2026) showed that LLMs performed poorly in generating species range maps and offered only limited improvement over random guessing in threat classification. Comparable effects have been observed in other AI domains, where imbalances in training data have produced systematically poorer model performance for underrepresented groups (Birhane, 2022). Together, these examples illustrate how unbalanced training data can transfer existing knowledge gaps into model outputs, highlighting the importance of identifying, documenting, and reducing such biases before models are applied beyond their validated domain. AI models can furthermore introduce subtler epistemic risks (Loru et al. 2025), including the confident fabrication of ecological information, the misrepresentation of species-trait responses to environmental gradients, and the generation of unsupported ecological interactions or spatial patterns. In ecological applications, documented limitations already include errors in quantitative information extraction and uneven performance across tasks (Gougherty and Clipp, 2024, Dorm et al. 2026). For these reasons, responsible openness and transparent governance of ecological data and metadata are vital, because the reliability of specialized models and large-scale synthesis depends on whether foundational ecological resources can be appropriately accessed, documented, and independently evaluated. Reproducible evaluation therefore requires practical commitments. Ecological AI studies should provide standardized documentation describing where their training data came from, which taxa, regions, and environmental conditions they cover, how the model is intended to be used, and its known limitations. Established tools such as datasheets for datasets and model cards can support this documentation (Gebru et al. 2021). Models should also be evaluated across taxa, regions, languages, and environmental conditions, and data, code, prompts, model weights, and independent evaluation sets should be released where ethically, legally, and technically possible (Maasri et al. 2022, Smith et al. 2024). In order to improve data exchange and utilization, general principles and standards for the creation, verification, and sharing of data should be established while respecting the owners and creators of specific databases. Any restrictions and access procedures should also be documented. Public initiatives such as the Minerva LLM (Orlando et al. 2024) illustrate the value of transparent, language-specific model development, but openness alone does not ensure ecological or cultural validity across regions. AI also changes the politics of openness by creating a risk that openly shared data and open-source code are incorporated into proprietary models without reciprocal access, attribution, credit, or participation for the researchers, developers, and communities who produced them. In public and public/private programs such as GenAI4EU (2025), adequate funding should mean sustained support for data curation, digitization of legacy records, targeted collection in documented gaps, local skills and infrastructure, and independent auditing, not only model development. Funders, publishers, scientific societies, and research institutions should recognize data curation as a research output and require transparent documentation and evaluation. Collaboration should connect local communities and data holders to national infrastructures, international repositories, and standards bodies. Identifying and reducing bias in AI development, enabling robust validation, and sustaining open infrastructures all depend fundamentally on the availability of high-quality, representative, and well-documented ecological data. Where data are scarce, uneven, or unreliable, transparency becomes especially important for identifying gaps and assessing their consequences (Titley et al. 2017). Open data and governance policies must therefore be accompanied by dedicated funding for targeted data collection, the digitization of legacy records, curation, metadata preparation, quality control, local computational infrastructure, training, and equitable collaboration, particularly in under-sampled regions. Such investments are necessary to prevent openness from disproportionately benefiting institutions that already possess the resources needed to exploit shared datasets. Openness should not, however, imply unrestricted public release. Precise locations of threatened species, Indigenous and local knowledge, and data governed by consent or legal agreements may require spatial generalization, controlled access, embargoes, or community authority (Tulloch et al. 2018). Data should instead be as open as possible and as protected as necessary, combining FAIR data stewardship with the CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics) where Indigenous or community-governed data are involved. International coordination among funders, ecological societies, repositories, publishers, data providers, and model developers is also needed to establish interoperable standards for data collection, annotation, documentation, sharing, and controlled access. Differences in the quality, resolution, and accessibility of ecological datasets should be explicitly documented and considered during model development and evaluation rather than remaining hidden (Dwivedi et al. 2022). Without shared standards and a commitment to responsible openness, ecological AI risks becoming fragmented, opaque, and shaped primarily by actors with the greatest computational and data resources. The practical priorities that we highlight are the following. Ecologists, AI researchers, funders, journals, repositories, and ecological societies should: audit geographic, taxonomic, temporal, and, where relevant, linguistic gaps in AI training and evaluation data, and quantify their effects on model performance; fund targeted data collection and the digitization of legacy records where these gaps have meaningful consequences; require machine-readable metadata and licenses, provenance records, uncertainty documentation, datasheets for datasets, and model cards; maintain independent benchmark datasets stratified across regions, taxa, sensors, and environmental conditions; and ensure that data-producing communities have access to computational infrastructure, training, credit, and decision-making roles rather than being treated solely as data providers (Wilkinson et al. 2016, Smith et al. 2024). Ecological research stands at a decisive crossroad: As AI reshapes how we observe and interpret the natural world, the openness and responsible governance of our data, models, and publications will determine whether this transformation is equitable and scientifically robust. Unrepresentative datasets, or data and models that cannot be independently evaluated, risk narrowing ecological insight, reinforcing global disparities, and introducing epistemic distortions that degrade our collective understanding of ecological systems. A well-governed, participatory, and inclusive ecological knowledge system, open where possible and protected where necessary, supported by public LLM research, auditable domain-specific models, and genuinely accessible publishing practices, is crucial to ensure that AI becomes a tool for discovery and justice rather than distortion. Just as copyleft preserved the freedoms to use, modify, and share software, responsible openness can free environmental science from informational silos while respecting legitimate restrictions. In the age of AI, openness is not only a technical requirement but an ethical obligation: Shared and responsibly governed knowledge is the foundation of collective solutions. items.title: Operationalizing biological interpretability in health-related visual stimuli using multimodal artificial intelligence as standardized non-human raters
items.abstract: Abstract Evaluation and assessment research in health communication requires structured, construct-based approaches for interpreting visual materials. This study introduces the Asclepius Biological Interpretability Scale, developed through a two-stage modified Delphi process (a joint image-and-item panel followed by an independent item-only panel) grounded in the Biopsychosocial Model and Visual Literacy Theory, and examines whether multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) systems can reproducibly apply this framework relative to internally generated human reference scores. Six artworks (four health-themed and two controls) were evaluated by three multimodal AI models and four researchers (internal human reference) using a standardized protocol with independent researcher-operated accounts, memory-isolation procedures, repeated assessments over two days, and the final 20-item scale. Because Image Type varied across only six stimuli, health-themed versus control differences were summarized at the image level (Cohen’s d), human–AI differences were summarized descriptively at the rater level, and reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Spearman correlations. Within this development image set, AI-generated scores were descriptively higher for health-themed than for control images on the three biomedical subscales (image-level Cohen’s d = 0.91–1.38) but not on Non-Medical Interpretability (d = 0.49); with four health-themed and two control images, these differences were not statistically significant ( p = 0.19–0.60). Reproducibility across researcher-operated accounts was excellent for the three biomedical subscales (ICC = 0.90–0.97) and moderate for Non-Medical Interpretability (ICC = 0.57), whereas agreement across assessment days was poor (ICC = 0.04–0.46). The four researchers’ internal reference scores were higher than the AI-generated scores on the biomedical subscales for health-themed images (mean differences 1.41–1.96 points) and lower on Non-Medical Interpretability (− 2.02 to − 2.19 points). These findings provide preliminary methodological evidence that multimodal AI can reproducibly apply a structured interpretability framework to controlled visual stimuli. Although day-to-day stability and the Non-Medical Interpretability subscale, which showed substantial internal-consistency problems, require further refinement, the results support the feasibility of using AI as standardized non-human raters within controlled methodological settings. Broader validation using authentic health communication materials and independent external human raters remains necessary.

items.title: Optimizing ergonomics and productivity in automotive assembly lines: a bi-objective integer linear programming approach
items.abstract: Abstract The automotive industry’s operations face a critical dilemma: achieving high productivity while maintaining adequate ergonomic standards. High-volume production amplifies this condition, because the frequency of task execution keeps ergonomic risk ever-present. This work presents a real case from an automotive body parts assembly line. The objectives are to minimize the maximum individual ergonomic risk throughout job-rotation periods along a daily journey, and to optimize productivity by determining the optimal worker-to-workstation assignments. The Occupational Repetitive Action (OCRA) index is used to assess the risk of upper extremity musculoskeletal disorders. To solve this bi-objective problem, two algorithms are proposed: an $$\varepsilon $$ ε -constraint approach and a Tchebychev method. Both are grounded in a novel Integer Linear Programming (ILP) model tailored to integrate ergonomic and productivity considerations. The algorithms generated a complete Pareto front of 16 efficient solutions within a reasonable computational time. Managerial insights are derived, highlighting the inherent trade-off between the makespan and ergonomic risk, providing valuable guidelines for balancing worker well-being and productivity in assembly-line operations.

items.title: Organizational Readiness In Artificial Intelligence Implementation: The Role of Digital Transformation In Bank Indonesia
items.abstract: This study analyzes the relationship between digitalization, structural transformation, and carbon emission intensity in six ASEAN countries, namely Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam, and Cambodia. The study uses annual panel data for the period 2004–2024, with the main estimation period covering 2010–2024. Carbon emission intensity is used as the dependent variable, while the number of internet users, industry value added, urban population, GDP per capita, international trade, and services sector value added are used as independent variables. All variables are transformed into natural logarithms so that the coefficients can be interpreted as elasticities. Estimation is conducted using the Fixed Effects Model with period fixed effects and Panel EGLS with period weights following model selection tests. The results show that digitalization, proxied by the number of internet users, has a positive but statistically insignificant relationship with carbon emission intensity. In contrast, industry value added, urban population, GDP per capita, and international trade have positive and significant relationships. Services sector value added has a negative and significant relationship with carbon emission intensity. These findings indicate that structural transformation toward the services sector is associated with lower emission intensity, while industrial expansion, urbanization, economic growth, and trade are associated with increased carbon emission intensity in the countries examined.

items.title: PAI Students’ Perceptions of Ethics in the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Learning
items.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) for learning in higher education supports information retrieval, understanding of learning materials, reference searches, and the completion of academic assignments. However, its use raises ethical concerns regarding academic honesty, responsibility, critical thinking skills, and potential dependence on technology. This study aimed to describe Pendidikan Agama Islam (PAI) students’ perceptions of the ethics of AI use in learning at UIN Sjech M. Djamil Djambek Bukittinggi. The study employed a descriptive qualitative approach involving three PAI students as primary informants and two lecturers as supporting informants, selected based on their relevance to the research focus. Data were collected through interviews, observations, and documentation, then analyzed using Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña’s model through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings showed that students viewed AI as a tool that made learning easier, with its use requiring information verification, an understanding of sources, and critical thinking. AI use considered ethical included refraining from copying answers directly, conducting independent analysis, and maintaining AI’s role as a support for the thinking process. These findings underscore the importance of AI literacy, academic integrity, and students’ responsibility in PAI learning. This study provides a contextual account of students’ ethical perceptions and offers input for students, lecturers, and the study program to develop critical and responsible use of AI.

items.title: Pemberdayaan Pokdarwis Melalui Layanan Suara Berbasis AI di Desa Wisata Kelawi
items.abstract: Kelawi Tourism Village, South Lampung, has strong community-based tourism potential, but the Minang Rua Bahari Tourism Awareness Group (Pokdarwis) faces communication barriers when serving international visitors. This Community Service Program (PKM) aimed to strengthen Pokdarwis capacity through an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted voice service as a communication support tool. The program was conducted from 12 to 14 June 2026 and involved 15 Pokdarwis members. Activities included problem identification, local knowledge development and validation, QR-based service implementation, training, mentoring, and evaluation at four service points: visitor reception, turtle conservation, Green Canyon, and homestay and culinary services. Results showed an increase in partner capacity from 58.2% in the pre-test to 91.8% in the post-test, representing a 33.6 percentage-point improvement. Participant satisfaction reached 92%, while partner and visitor achievement rates reached 95.2% and 94.5%, respectively. The program demonstrates that AI can support communication, conservation, safety, and the delivery of local cultural and culinary information without replacing the role of Pokdarwis.

items.abstract: This study aimed to examine the effect of intrinsic motivation on students' active participation in extracurricular activities at SMK Negeri 7 Makassar. A quantitative approach with a causal associative research design was employed. The population consisted of 256 students participating in extracurricular activities, with a sample of 155 students selected using proportionate stratified random sampling. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression analysis. The findings showed that both intrinsic motivation and students' active participation were categorized as high. The regression analysis revealed that intrinsic motivation had a positive and significant effect on students' active participation, with a significance value of 0.000 (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the coefficient of determination (R² = 0.247) indicated that intrinsic motivation contributed 24.7% to students' active participation, while the remaining 75.3% was influenced by other factors beyond the scope of this study. These findings indicate that higher levels of intrinsic motivation are associated with higher levels of students' active participation in extracurricular activities.

items.abstract: Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) is an essential component of practical learning in the Electric Power Network Engineering (TJTL) program because students are exposed to electrical and workshop hazards. This study aimed to develop an OHS educational video and determine its feasibility, student response, and the increase in students’ understanding after use. The study employed Research and Development (R&D) with the 4-D model consisting of Define, Design, Develop, and Disseminate. Product validation involved three expert validators consisting of one media expert and two OHS experts, while user feasibility was assessed by three teacher practitioners. Student response involved 29 students, and the increase in understanding was examined using a one-group pretest-posttest design and N-Gain analysis. The mean feasibility score was 4.50 from the expert-media assessment and 4.82 from the practitioner assessment, both in the “very good” category. Student response reached a mean score of 4.78, also in the “very good” category. The mean N-Gain was 0.86, classified as high, indicating a substantial increase in test scores after the video was used. The findings support the use of the video as a contextual learning aid for OHS preparation before TJTL practical activities. However, the effectiveness evidence is limited because the study used one group without a comparison group and measured cognitive understanding rather than actual safety behavior.

items.title: Perceptions of Academic Staff on the Integration of AI and Digital Connectivity for Transformative Educational Management in Bayelsa State
items.abstract: The study assessed the perceptions of academic staff on the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital connectivity for transformative educational management in tertiary institutions in Bayelsa State. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, guided by two research questions. The population comprised academic staff from selected public universities and colleges of education in Bayelsa State, from which a sample of 350 respondents was drawn using stratified random sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire titled Artificial Intelligence and Digital Connectivity in Educational Management Questionnaire (AIDEMQ), validated by experts and yielding a reliability coefficient of 0.89 via Cronbach's alpha. Descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) were used to answer the research questions. The findings revealed that academic staff generally perceived AI as enhancing administrative efficiency through improved decision-making, error reduction, transparency, and time management, although challenges such as inadequate training and limited practical application constrained its full potential. Similarly, digital connectivity was perceived as effective in improving communication, collaboration, information dissemination, and the quality of teaching and learning, though gaps in infrastructure and system functionality limited its impact on administrative planning and scheduling. The study concluded that while AI and digital connectivity hold significant potential for transforming educational management, targeted interventions including capacity building, infrastructure enhancement, and strategic system integration are necessary to fully realize these benefits. Recommendations included providing regular staff training, investing in robust digital infrastructure, and implementing supportive policies to optimize the integration of AI and digital tools in tertiary institutions.

items.title: Performance uncertainty in medical image analysis: A large-scale investigation of confidence intervals
items.abstract: Performance uncertainty quantification is essential for reliable validation and eventual clinical translation of medical imaging artificial intelligence (AI). Confidence intervals (CIs) play a central role in this process by indicating how precise a reported performance estimate is. Yet, due to the limited amount of work examining CI behavior in medical imaging, the community remains largely unaware of how many diverse CI methods exist and how they behave in specific settings. The purpose of this study is to close this gap. To this end, we conducted a large-scale empirical analysis across a total of 24 segmentation and classification tasks, using 19 trained models per task group, a broad spectrum of commonly used performance metrics, multiple aggregation strategies, and several widely adopted CI methods. Reliability (coverage) and precision (width) of each CI method were estimated across all settings to characterize their dependence on study characteristics. Our analysis revealed five principal findings: (1) the sample size required for reliable CIs varies from a few dozens to several thousands of cases depending on study parameters; (2) CI behavior is strongly affected by the choice of performance metric; (3) aggregation strategy substantially influences the reliability of CIs, e.g. they require more observations for macro than for micro; (4) the machine learning problem (segmentation versus classification) modulates these effects; (5) different CI methods are not equally reliable and precise depending on the use case. Finally, we derived practical implications of this study in the form of a decision tree which shall prove useful to the community. This paves the way for future consensus guidelines on reporting performance uncertainty.
